title: Build a clock
text: When no published clock fits your assay or your question, fit one to your cohort. FALCONAge compares several learners first, every number out of fold, and then fits the one you choose.

title: Build a clock
text:
1. Compare learners

PythonR


import falconage as fa

d   = fa.prepare(fa.read_betas("betas.csv"))      # obs must hold the target, e.g. "age"
cmp = fa.compare_learners(d, target="age", groups="person")

cmp.table          # one row per learner: MAE, MedAE, r, slope, bias by thirds, seconds
cmp.selected       # the nested error of "pick the best": the number to report
cmp.best           # the learner with the lowest out-of-fold MAE


library(FALCONAge)

d   <- prepare(read_betas("betas.csv"))
cmp <- compare_learners(d, target = "age", groups = "person")

cmp$table
cmp$selected



groups names a sample-sheet column whose members always stay on the same side of a split: the person, when there are repeated visits, or the batch or cohort, for leave-one-group-out. Without it, a person’s second visit is predicted by a model that was trained on their first.

title: Build a clock
text:
2. The learners









Name
What it is
Writes a clock file
Needs




elasticnet
glmnet’s elastic net, alpha 0.5, lambda by inner cross-validation
yes
nothing extra


lasso, ridge
the same with alpha 1 and 0
yes
nothing extra


screened_elasticnet
the 2,000 CpGs most correlated with the target, then elastic net; the screen runs inside each training part
yes
nothing extra


pc_elasticnet
principal components, then elastic net; maps back to one weight per CpG
yes
nothing extra


random_forest, gradient_boosting, svr, mlp
scikit-learn regressors
no
pip install "falconage[learn]" (in the Docker image already)



Pass transform="horvath" to fit Horvath’s log-linear transform of age and invert it, which matters when the cohort includes children.

title: Build a clock
text:
3. Read the comparison honestly

Quote selected, not the best row of table. Picking the best of several learners is itself a fitted choice, so the winner’s own error is optimistic. selected repeats the pick inside each outer fold and measures it on samples the pick never saw.
Look at the slope and the bias by thirds, not only MAE. Every penalised model pulls predictions towards the mean, so the old read young and the young read old.
The most accurate age predictor is not necessarily the best biomarker. Test the residual against an outcome on a cohort the model was not fitted on.

title: Build a clock
section: 4. Fit the chosen learner and save it
text:
4. Fit the chosen learner and save it

PythonR


fit = fa.fit_clock(d, target="age", learner="pc_elasticnet", groups="person")
fit.metrics                        # out-of-fold MAE, MedAE, r, slope
fit.to_clock("mycohortclock", "my_clocks/")


fit <- fit_clock(d, target = "age", learner = "pc_elasticnet", groups = "person")
fit$metrics
clock_to_file(fit, "mycohortclock", "my_clocks/")



to_clock writes mycohortclock.yaml, its coefficients and its reference values into my_clocks/. Add a clock scores it like any catalogue clock.
→ Why it works this way: Building a clock

title: Stack clocks
text: A stack learns weights for several clocks’ scores, out of fold, and reports the result next to the best single clock and the plain mean measured the same way, so the gain (or its absence) is visible.

title: Stack clocks
text:
1. Fit a stack

PythonR


res = fa.score(d, clocks="compatible")
st  = fa.stack_clocks(res, target="age",
                      clocks=["horvath2013", "hannum", "dnamphenoage", "zhangen"],
                      method="nnls")

st.weights        # one weight per clock, on standardised scores
st.metrics        # out-of-fold MAE, MedAE, r, slope
st.comparison     # each clock alone, and the plain mean, measured the same way


res <- score(d, clocks = "compatible")
st  <- stack_clocks(res, target = "age",
                    clocks = c("horvath2013", "hannum", "dnamphenoage", "zhangen"),
                    method = "nnls")
st$weights
st$comparison

title: Stack clocks
text:
2. Choose a method








method
What it does
Allowed when




"mean"
The plain average of the scores
Every clock has the same scale type


"nnls"
Non-negative weights on standardised scores (default)
Always


"ridge"
Ridge-penalised weights on standardised scores
Always


"cox"
A Cox model on the scores; target is follow-up time and event_col the event
You have survival data



A plain mean of years and a pace has no unit, so it is refused; the learned methods standardise each clock and take the scale of the target. First-generation clocks are strongly correlated with each other, which is why the weights come from non-negative least squares or ridge.

title: Stack clocks
text:
3. Save it as a clock
st.to_clock("mystack", "my_clocks/")
When every clock in the stack is a weighted sum of CpGs followed by constant shifts and scalings, the stack is itself a weighted sum over all their CpGs. It is written as one coefficient file that Add a clock scores like any other, with coverage checks and a technical standard error. A stack containing a clock with a nonlinear output (Horvath’s anti-log, a sigmoid) stays in the session: use st.predict(res).
One difference to know: a CpG your data lacks, and that no clock in the stack publishes a reference value for, is filled with the mean of the present CpGs. For the combined clock that mean is taken over all of its CpGs rather than each clock’s own, so on data missing such CpGs the collapsed clock and st.predict(res) can differ slightly. warnings.csv names every such fill.

title: Stack clocks
section: Do not test a group difference on the samples the stack was fitted on
text:
Do not test a group difference on the samples the stack was fitted on
A stack fitted on the same samples you then compare between groups has already seen the answer. Fit it on one set and test on another. To ask whether a group difference holds across clocks, use fa.consensus() instead (Age acceleration): it tests rather than fits.

title: Your first run
text: This page assumes the image is installed (Install). Every command is run from the folder that holds your data, and the output is written to that same folder.

title: Your first run
text:
1. Run the demo
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu demo
It writes a small synthetic dataset (40 samples, labelled as synthetic in every file), runs the whole pipeline on it, and prints:

read 40 sample(s) x 325375 feature(s) on 450K
scored 53 clock(s); 119 skipped
  consensus: unsupported
  31 figure(s)
49 note(s) about individual clocks: falconage_demo/results/warnings.csv

done. Open falconage_demo/results/report.html

The values are random draws with an age trend, so the ages in the report are not meaningful. Its purpose is to show every output file before you run your own data.

title: Your first run
text:
2. Output files







File
What it holds




report.html
The report: open this first. Scores, uncertainty, acceleration, the figures, and every note


scores.csv
One row per sample per clock, with the clock’s scale and unit


scores_wide.csv
The same scores as a table, samples by clocks


technical_se.csv
How much of each score is measurement noise (a standard error per score)


conformal_interval.csv
A prediction interval per score, for clocks with a published calibration


acceleration.csv
Age acceleration per sample, where the sample sheet gives age and the clock’s scale allows it


consensus.csv, consensus_verdict.txt
Whether a difference between groups holds across clocks, when there is a group column


interpretation.csv
What each clock measures, its unit, and which arithmetic its scale permits


evidence.csv
Published reliability and validation results for each clock, with DOIs


qc.csv, qc_per_sample.csv
Feature coverage per clock and quality checks per sample


skipped_clocks.csv
Every clock not scored, with the reason


warnings.csv
Notes about individual clocks: tissue mismatches, imputed probes, known paper discrepancies


run_manifest.json
Versions, the SHA-256 of every coefficient file used, and the settings: enough to reproduce the run


figures/
Every figure in the report as its own PNG

title: Your first run
text:
3. Run your own data
Put the data in the current folder and name it on the command line:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu run betas.csv --samples samples.csv
The output is written to betas_falconage/; --outdir sets another folder.
The input is preprocessed, quality-controlled data in one of these formats:



You have
Give run




A beta matrix (samples by probes, or probes by samples)
betas.csv, .tsv, .parquet or .h5ad


A GEO series matrix
GSE12345_series_matrix.txt.gz


Clinical chemistry
labs.csv --kind clinical (units are declared in the file)


A Nightingale NMR export
nmr.xlsx --kind nightingale



The sample sheet is optional but worth having. Its first column is the sample id, exactly as in the data, and any of these columns are used:
sample_id,age,sex,tissue,group
S001,34.5,F,whole blood,control
S002,61.0,M,whole blood,case







Column
Enables




age
Age acceleration, and agreement of each clock with age


tissue
The check that each clock was fitted on your specimen type


group
The test of whether a group difference holds across clocks


sex
Sex-specific clocks and the sex check on X-linked probes



Without a sample sheet the run still scores every clock; it says which steps it skipped and why.
Choosing clocks. By default run scores every clock your data supports. To score named ones:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu \
  run betas.csv --samples samples.csv --clocks horvath2013,hannum,dnamphenoage
falconage clocks list shows every id, and Choosing a clock helps pick.

title: Your first run
text:
4. In a pipeline
run is built to be called unattended by a workflow manager such as Nextflow or Snakemake:
falconage run betas.csv --samples samples.csv --outdir results --format tsv \
  --threads 4 --log-file results.log
falconage versions --process FALCONAGE_RUN > versions.yml







Option or behaviour
What it gives a pipeline




--threads N
Caps the numerical thread pools at the CPUs the task was given


--format tsv
Tab-separated output tables


--log-level {quiet,info,debug}, --log-file
Progress on stdout, log records on stderr and in the file


Exit status
0 success, 1 internal error, 2 usage error, 3 input data error, 4 scoring or analysis error


falconage versions --process NAME
The YAML a versions.yml takes


The image
Passes an absolute-path command (/bin/bash .command.sh) straight through, ships ps for task metrics, and runs as any user id



An error prints one line naming the cause, for example falconage: error: input not found: betas.csv; --log-level debug adds the traceback.

title: Your first run
section: The same in Python or R
text:
The same in Python or R

PythonR


import falconage as fa

data = fa.prepare(fa.read_betas("betas.csv"))
res  = fa.score(data, clocks="compatible")

res.summary()
fa.acceleration(res, method="both")
fa.plot.ba_vs_ca(res, "horvath2013")
fa.report.write_report(res, "report.html")


library(FALCONAge)

d   <- prepare(read_betas("betas.csv"))
res <- score(d, clocks = "compatible")

summary(res)
acceleration(res, method = "both")
plot_ba_vs_ca(res, "horvath2013")
report(res, "report.html")



Both produce the same numbers, because both run the same code. The R package delegates all arithmetic to the Python core through reticulate, and the R suite asserts equality at tolerance exactly zero rather than approximate agreement.

title: Your first run
text:
Scoring
Every Python and R snippet from here on runs unchanged in three places: inside the Docker image (docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu python, or ... R), in a native install, or in the CLI-free path below. Only the way you open the session differs.

PythonR


d   = fa.prepare(fa.read_betas("betas.csv"))
res = fa.score(d, clocks="compatible")

res.summary()
res.scores               # samples x clocks
res.long()               # one row per sample per clock, with the scale
res.qc()                 # per-clock feature coverage and skip reasons
res.manifest             # versions, precision, SHA-256 of every coefficient file


d   <- prepare(read_betas("betas.csv"))
res <- score(d, clocks = "compatible")

summary(res)
as.data.frame(res)                  # samples x clocks
as.data.frame(res, form = "long")   # one row per sample per clock, with the scale
coverage(res)                       # per-clock feature coverage and skip reasons
manifest(res)                       # versions, precision, and every coefficient checksum



clocks = "compatible" scores what this dataset can support and reports the rest as skipped with a reason. Naming clocks explicitly is different: then every one must work, because an explicit request should never be dropped quietly.

title: Your first run
text:
Interpreting the result
The scale, the unit, which arithmetic is permitted, both coverage measures, the published reliability where one exists, and any documented disagreement between the clock’s paper and the coefficients in circulation, all on the object rather than only on this website:

PythonR


res.interpretation()


interpretation(res)



technical_icc and biological_icc are separate columns because they measure different things and do not track together: the same sample assayed twice, versus the same person sampled again a few days later. A clock can be excellent on the first and poor on the second, and the clocks most used to claim an intervention worked are where that gap is widest.

title: Install
text:
One image carries Python, R, the falconage command and every bundled clock at pinned versions, so the same input gives the same numbers on any machine. Nothing else needs installing.
1. Install Docker. Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. Start it, then check it answers:
docker --version
“command not found” or “cannot connect to the Docker daemon” means Docker is not installed or not running; nothing below works until it is.
2. Get the image:
docker pull bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu
3. Check it:
docker run --rm bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu config

FALCONAge 1.0.0
  registry     1.1.0  (68 human clocks, 68 score offline)
  numpy        2.5.1
  cpu cores    8

That is the whole install. Your first run is the next step.










Tag
Contains
Use it when




1.0.0-cpu (also latest)
Python, R, the command line, every reader
Almost always


1.0.0-py
Python and the command line; no R, and no parquet or .h5ad reader
You only use Python or the command line, on CSV, TSV, GEO series, clinical or NMR files, and want a smaller download






"$PWD" in the commands on this site means “the folder I am in now”, and it is spelled differently in each shell:



Where you are typing
Write




macOS Terminal, Linux, Git Bash, WSL
"$PWD"


Windows PowerShell
"${PWD}"


Windows cmd.exe
"%cd%"



A path error on Windows is almost always this.
The image’s entrypoint is the falconage command, so the first word after the image name is a verb: demo, run, config, clocks. The exceptions are python, R, Rscript and bash, which open that program inside the image:
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu python
docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu R
On Linux, if the run cannot write into your folder (“Permission denied”), run the container as yourself by adding -u "$(id -u):$(id -g)" after docker run --rm.



Nothing bundled needs the network. Public data fetched with falconage download is cached. Add a named volume so a new container does not fetch it again:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -v falconage-cache:/opt/falconage/cache \
  bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu download GSE40279



Both images are published, so pulling is the two-minute route:

title: Install
text:
One image carries Python, R, the falconage command and every bundled clock at pinned versions, so the same input gives the same numbers on any machine. Nothing else needs installing.
1. Install Docker. Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. Start it, then check it answers:
docker --version
“command not found” or “cannot connect to the Docker daemon” means Docker is not installed or not running; nothing below works until it is.
2. Get the image:
docker pull bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu
3. Check it:
docker run --rm bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu config

FALCONAge 1.0.0
  registry     1.1.0  (68 human clocks, 68 score offline)
  numpy        2.5.1
  cpu cores    8

That is the whole install. Your first run is the next step.










Tag
Contains
Use it when

Almost always

Where you are typing
Write

If you already manage your own Python or R environment.

text:
When something looks wrong
Run falconage config (or falconage_config() in R) first. It reports the version, the registry and how many clocks are usable, and it is the first thing to include in a bug report.

title: Preparing data and coverage
text:
FALCONAge does not normalise, filter probes or run sample QC. The input is a matrix that has already been through those steps upstream, for example in the methylarray pipeline, minfi or SeSAMe. What fa.prepare() (CLI: falconage prepare) applies is limited to what scoring requires: identifier harmonisation, EPIC v2 replicate collapse, clipping to the beta range and platform detection.
Rows are samples, columns are features. Feature names are the identifiers the clock coefficients use: cg00000029 for methylation probes, and the declared analyte names for clinical chemistry and NMR. fa.FalconData holds the matrix in X, sample metadata (age, sex, tissue, group) in obs, and per-feature annotation in var; it reads and writes AnnData’s .h5ad.



EPIC v2 column names look like cg00000029_TC21. fa.prepare() strips the suffix and averages replicate probes of the same CpG before anything else. Skipping this means every clock sees almost no overlapping features on EPIC v2 data.



Stage 1 - dataset-level, before the clock. fa.preprocess.impute() with median (default), mean or none, run only when asked.
Stage 2 - clock-level, for features the dataset does not contain at all. Filling with zero in beta space means “fully unmethylated”, which is biologically wrong for most sites, so FALCONAge never does it.
What FALCONAge does, and what the R packages do. For a linear clock FALCONAge fills an absent feature with the mean of the clock’s observed features over the whole dataset: one constant, the same for every absent feature and every sample (models/linear.py). imputation="reference" replaces it with a per-feature value wherever a reference is supplied. The mitotic mean, percentile and transmission clocks (epiTOC1/2/3, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper/Hypo, stemTOC, stemTOCvitro) are the exception: their published statistic is taken over the sites present, so FALCONAge leaves absent sites out and records imputation: "excluded". methylclock 1.16.0 leaves absent CpGs out of the sum (predAge in R/internals.R), which is a fill of 0. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 fills each one with its per-probe mean from the package’s golden_ref table (meanImputation, called from methyAge). Each policy adds the same amount to every sample, so on one dataset the packages differ by a constant
Δ = Σ_{j absent} w_j (f_j − g_j)
where w_j is the coefficient and f_j, g_j are the two fills. For Horvath’s clocks the constant is multiplied by 21 above the adult age of 20, where the anti-log transform is linear.
On a dataset that lacks some of a clock’s CpGs, the packages in circulation fill them differently (methylclock and dnaMethyAge among them), and that alone can move the same clock’s age by several years between packages that agree on every coefficient and intercept. Given identical complete input there is no difference to explain: the conformance suite in test/conformance/ scores 75 clock-package pairs on the same filled matrix, and every difference left over is traced to a coefficient copy that departs from its primary source. The offsets belong to a dataset’s missing CpGs, not to the clocks, so the registry does not carry them as per-clock discrepancies. The coverage record (res.coverage[clock_id]) gives the number of values filled (n_imputed) and the method (imputation). Neither 0 nor a pooled mean is a published value for a CpG, which is why a per-CpG reference from each clock’s own training data is the better fill.
Horvath’s normalisation is optional in his own code, and the packages default differently. Horvath 2013 supplied a calibration step (Additional file 24, BMIQcalibration): each sample’s betas over 21,368 probes are mapped onto the distribution of goldstandard2, the per-probe means in Additional file 22 (Genome Biology, CC BY 2.0), after absent probes are set to those means. dnaMethyAge 0.2.0 runs it by default for HorvathS2013 (simple_mode = TRUE skips it), methylclock 1.16.0 does not (normalize = FALSE), and FALCONAge offers it as an opt-in step, fa.preprocess.horvath_normalise() (R: horvath_normalise()). The step mostly moves the level of Horvath 2013 age rather than the ranking of samples, so a comparison across packages has to say whether it ran.
horvath_normalise() is a port of BMIQcalibration. The R code fits its beta mixtures on 20,000 probes drawn by set.seed(1); sample(...) and stops its optimisers early (Nelder-Mead after 50 evaluations), so its result depends on the exact draw and the exact optimiser path; the port reproduces each piece as R computes it (the Mersenne-Twister draw, optim’s Nelder-Mead and BFGS, RPMM’s blc, density()). Against the unmodified Additional file 24 it agrees to 3e-10 in beta on a synthetic fixture and to 2e-8 years of Horvath age on the 120 samples above, reproducing the −1.87-year shift. Two arguments follow the code people actually ran:








Argument
Default
The other value




absent
"drop": calibrate on the gold-standard probes the data carry, as Knight et al.’s published wrapper does
"fill": set absent probes to their gold-standard value first


sample_kind
"Rejection": R 3.6.0 and later
"Rounding": the draw of earlier R



With sample_kind="Rounding", Knight et al.’s own test dataset gives 37.3665, 38.3463 and 39.322 weeks against the 37.366, 38.346 and 39.324 their instructions state; the remaining 0.002 is their k-nearest-neighbour imputation of 51 missing values. Only the 21,368 gold-standard probes are changed, and a missing value is set to its gold-standard value first, as Horvath’s code does for a single sample; both counts are recorded in uns["horvath_normalisation"].
Reporting the imputation method alongside a score is not optional; it changes the answer, and the run manifest records it.



These are per-clock and must run after feature selection, not before:







Step
Clocks in the catalogue




robust scale (x − median)/std
AltumAge


per-sample z-score across features
ZhangEN, ZhangBLUP


mean over non-missing
epiTOC1, HypoClock, EPICmitHyper, EPICmitHypo


0.95 quantile over non-missing
stemTOC, stemTOCvitro


nan → 0
epiTOC2, epiTOC3


NaN → reference value
most linear clocks

title: Preparing data and coverage
text:
Methylation clock coverage

Coverage across the genome
Every falconage run on methylation data draws this figure first, before any clock is scored. It is written to figures/clock_coverage_across_the_genome.png, with its legend text in the .txt file beside it, and includes clocks added with --clocks-dir.






Figure 1: Clock coverage across the genome. Every DNA methylation clock in FALCONAge, one track each, with its CpGs at their positions on the genome (hg19). Coloured where the EPIC v1 array carries the CpG, grey where it does not; the legend gives each clock’s colour and the share of its CpGs on the array. CpGs aligned across tracks are shared between clocks.



Python: fa.plot.clock_coverage_manhattan(data), or platform="EPICv2" without data. R: plot_clock_coverage().


Coverage and weight per clock
probe_loss() reports, per clock, how many features are present and how much of the model’s weight they carry. The second number is the one that detects EPIC v2 probe loss:

PythonR


fa.probe_loss(d, clocks="scoreable")


probe_loss(d, clocks = "scoreable")




                   tier  n_features  n_present  coverage  mass_coverage  bias_years          heaviest_absent
horvath2013     bundled         353        339    0.9603         0.9715     -1.2570   cg11932564 (0.8%), ...
hannum          bundled          71         64    0.9014         0.8994      1.0279   cg21139312 (2.7%), ...
zhangmortality  bundled          10          9    0.9000         0.7687      0.0124  cg08362785 (23.1%), ...

Three rows of the table for the EPIC v2 series in the test corpus (GSE330325). zhangmortality has nine of its ten CpGs, 90% by count, and the one it lacks carries 23% of its weight.
bias_years is filled in when the platform is one the shift has been measured on; see what probe loss costs. NaN there means not measured, never no bias.
A clock at 96% feature coverage and 61% weight coverage has kept nearly all its probes and lost the ones that matter. The scoring floor applies to both measures, so this run would be refused with a message naming the heaviest absent probes rather than returning a confident number.


Clock CpGs removed by upstream probe QC
A clock CpG can be absent for two reasons. The array may not carry it (platform loss), or the array carried it and a probe filter removed it afterwards. FALCONAge separates the two with a table, bundled with the package, of which Illumina arrays (27K, 450K, EPIC v1, EPIC v2) carry each clock CpG (fa.preprocess.platform_probes()). When removed CpGs carry at least 1% of a clock’s absolute weight, score() raises a probe_qc warning naming the heaviest of them, and the coverage record gives n_removed_by_qc and qc_removed_mass.
SNP, cross-reactive and detection filters are designed for association studies. For clock scoring, pass the matrix taken before probe filtering: the clock weights were fitted on those probes, and an imputed value replaces each one that is removed.

title: Figures and reports
text:
Two documents, each one self-contained HTML file.
The one-page report is the scores, the run and a few figures, small enough to send:
write_results(res, "results/")
report(res, "report.html", group = "condition")
It is one file, inlined CSS, base64 figures, the table embedded, so it still works after somebody emails it, which is the only thing anybody does with a report.
The full run, step by step. run_report() runs quality control, scoring, technical error, prediction intervals, age acceleration, a consensus test across clocks when a group column is named, and the interpretation tables, and writes every deliverable into one directory: the same directory the report command writes. With quarto = TRUE it adds falconage_report.qmd, in which every file of that directory sits under the step that produced it, in the order a reader has to take them, because each step is only as reliable as the ones before it:







Step
What it holds




0. Provenance
versions, the coefficient file and SHA-256 behind each clock, precision, warnings


1. Input and quality control
per-sample missingness and beta distribution; the QC figures


2. Coverage
per-clock coverage by feature count and by coefficient weight; clocks not scored, and why


3. Scores
the scores, what each category of clock measures, and how the clocks relate


4. Agreement with chronological age
error against age and whether it depends on age


5. Uncertainty
technical standard error and conformal prediction intervals


6. Age acceleration
residuals on age, for the scales where they are defined


7. Group comparison
the consensus verdict and the test for every clock


8. Interpretation
what each score means and the published evidence, with DOIs


9. Further outputs
every other file in the directory, named and sized



A file the report does not recognise still appears, in step 9, so nothing in the directory is left out. Tables expand, search, page and download as CSV; figures enlarge on click and download at full resolution. Rendered, it is one HTML file with every figure and table embedded: 3.7 MB for 16 samples and three clocks.

PythonRCommand line


fa.report.run_report(d, "results/", group_col="condition", quarto=True)


run_report(d, "results/", group = "condition", quarto = TRUE)


docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu \
  report betas.csv --outdir results/ --group-col condition --quarto



Rendering it. Quarto is not in the FALCONAge image. Installed it takes 423 MB, which would add about 17% to the 2.5 GB image for an optional document, so inside the image the source is written and the run says so. Render it with the Quarto container, from the output directory, and open falconage_report.html:
cd results
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -e HOME=/tmp -v "$PWD:/w" -w /w \
  ghcr.io/quarto-dev/quarto quarto render falconage_report.qmd
Where Quarto is installed, run_report() renders it directly, and quarto_report("results/") (R) or fa.report.write_quarto_report("results/", render=True) (Python) rewrites the report for a directory that already exists.

title: Figures and reports
text:
Plots

What FALCONAge draws
Thirty-two figures in Python, twenty-one of them also in R, drawn alike because both languages read their colours, titles, subtitles and one-line descriptions from the same colorscheme.yaml. The gallery shows every one. The coverage map is drawn first on every run, before any clock is scored, and cannot be switched off. Every function returns its data frame as well as its figure, which is how two rendering engines draw the same numbers.
Ready for a manuscript. A figure carries its axes and its legend and nothing else: no title, no subtitle and no caption on the canvas, so it drops into a panel layout as it is. Each one is written as a pair named after its title, with the clock appended for per-clock figures:
figures/predicted_against_chronological_age_horvath2013.png
figures/predicted_against_chronological_age_horvath2013.txt
The .txt holds the title, the figure’s own numbers (n, r, MedAE and the like) and the description, ready to paste into a figure legend. save_figure() writes a pair from any figure you draw yourself, in Python (fa.plot.save_figure(fig, "figures")) and in R (save_figure(p, "figures")); figure_text() returns the same text as a list. Both reports show the title and description beneath each figure and link its .txt.







Figure
Answers




clock_coverage_manhattan
where every clock’s CpGs sit on the genome, which ones the data carries, and which clocks share them


ba_vs_ca
does this clock track age here, and with what bias


bland_altman
is the error age-dependent (regression dilution made visible)


calibration
is the predicted age calibrated across the age range


acceleration_by_group
do cases accelerate relative to controls


acceleration_density
the same, as distributions rather than summaries


acceleration_heatmap
clock × study, the whole pooled picture in one panel


forest
effect size with an interval, per clock


clock_corr
which clocks agree, clustered


clock_chord
how much of that agreement is shared CpGs rather than shared signal


clock_radar
one profile per group across clocks, on a common z scale


clock_pca, clock_embedding
sample structure in clock space; ageotypes


clock_scatter_matrix
pairwise acceleration, the plot_baa layout


coverage_bar, missingness
which clocks are scoring imputed values, read before the scores


beta_density
is the beta distribution bimodal, or did normalisation break


sex_check
does the X/Y dosage match the recorded sex


platform_comparison, study_comparison
is the batch bigger than the biology


benchmark_bars, benchmark_error_bias, benchmark_heatmap
AA1/AA2, the MedAE–MedE tradeoff, clock × dataset


timecourse, trajectory
clocks across a timepoint variable


clock_atlas
every clock, every pooled study, one figure



clock_chord is the one with no precedent in the list above and it earns its place: the correlation heatmap says two clocks agree, and the chord says how much of that agreement was built in by construction. A pair with a thick chord and a high correlation has told you much less than a pair with a high correlation and no chord at all.
A volcano plot of clock associations is implemented (fa.plot.volcano, R plot_volcano). GSEA (11) belongs to feature-level biology rather than to scoring, and spatial maps (12) wait on the spatial modality.
Two rules the code enforces rather than recommends. A figure whose data is empty, flat, or all zeros raises NothingToPlot and save_all records the reason, because an axis-free rectangle in a report reads as a measurement of nothing rather than as an absence of measurement. And the scale-type gate applies to figures too: a pace_ratio clock never reaches an acceleration panel.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Each of these is produced by test/run_all.py against the public test corpus and copied into test/output_figures/gallery/. They are regenerated from the code, so a figure here is what the current version actually draws – not a screenshot taken once.
The figures carry no title or caption on the canvas, only axes and legend, so they drop into a manuscript or a panel layout as they are. Each PNG is named after its title, and a .txt of the same name beside it holds the title, the figure’s own numbers and the description; the caption under each image here is read from that file. The same file’s ui block sets the colours and fonts of both HTML reports and of this site, so a figure, a report and a page of the documentation share one palette: Okabe-Ito for data, because group membership is carried by hue alone and has to survive colour-vision deficiency, and the logo orange, in a darker shade where it is text, only for links and controls.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Start here
Where every clock’s CpGs sit on the genome and which ones the array carries, then the question everyone actually has: which of these algorithms detects anything.

Clock coverage across the genome



Clock coverage across the genome


62 clocks · the EPICv1 array · mean coverage 98.0% · 41 fully covered.
One track per clock, every CpG at its position on the genome (hg19). In the clock’s colour, the data carries it; in grey, it does not. CpGs that line up across tracks are shared between clocks. Read this before the scores: a clock whose track is mostly grey is scored largely on filled values.
plot.clock_coverage_manhattan() in Python; written as clock_coverage_across_the_genome.png with clock_coverage_across_the_genome.txt.


Clock atlas across pooled studies



Clock atlas across pooled studies


40 clocks · 13 studies · 394 samples · 12 of 193 comparisons significant at BH q < 0.05.
Read panel D down the page. A row of hollow circles on zero is an algorithm that detected nothing in any cohort; filled dots pushed right are the ones that did, and a row with several says the effect held across studies rather than in one. Panels B and C are diagnostics for reading D, not scores: a clock that merely returned chronological age would be perfect in B, empty in D, and useless. Panel F separates the two ways of finding nothing: a clock that saw its features and detected no difference, from one that never had the features to look with. Panel G is for the clocks whose scale admits no acceleration at all (a pace, a telomere length, a division count) and asks the question their scale does allow: were cases and controls separated. Cliff’s delta, so 0 is no separation and 1 is complete, and unlike D it is not adjusted for age, which matters when a cohort’s cases are older than its controls.
plot.clock_atlas() in Python; written as clock_atlas_across_pooled_studies.png with clock_atlas_across_pooled_studies.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Is the clock calibrated
Before any biology: does the prediction track chronological age, and where does it drift.

Predicted against chronological age



Predicted against chronological age


altumage · n = 27 · r = 0.59 · MedAE = 45.45 years.
Distance from the dashed identity line is error, not acceleration; a clock sitting parallel to it but offset is biased, which MedE quantifies.
plot.ba_vs_ca() in Python; written as predicted_against_chronological_age.png with predicted_against_chronological_age.txt.


Agreement across the age range



Agreement across the age range


altumage · bias = 41.92 years · limits of agreement 21.8 to 62.1.
A trend in this cloud means the clock’s error depends on age, which a correlation coefficient cannot show and which invalidates a single MedAE.
plot.bland_altman() in Python; written as agreement_across_the_age_range.png with agreement_across_the_age_range.txt.


Residual against chronological age



Residual against chronological age


altumage · slope = +0.000 · a flat line at zero is perfect calibration.
A negative slope is regression to the mean: the clock over-ages the young and under-ages the old, which is the most common artefact in this field.
plot.calibration() in Python; written as residual_against_chronological_age.png with residual_against_chronological_age.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Age acceleration
The residual after age is removed, by group and across studies.

Age acceleration by group



Age acceleration by group


altumage · residual convention · AS vs HC.
Each point is one sample; the box is the median and interquartile range. Read the separation between groups, not the distance from zero.
plot.acceleration_by_group() in Python; written as age_acceleration_by_group.png with age_acceleration_by_group.txt.


Distribution of age acceleration



Distribution of age acceleration


altumage · residual convention · n = 28.
Counted, not smoothed: a kernel density on a dozen cases invents structure that is not in the data.
plot.acceleration_density() in Python; written as distribution_of_age_acceleration.png with distribution_of_age_acceleration.txt.


Age acceleration across clocks and samples



Age acceleration across clocks and samples


19 clocks x 394 samples · z-scored within clock.
Rows that disagree are clocks measuring different things; a column that is red everywhere is a sample, not a finding.
plot.acceleration_heatmap() in Python; written as age_acceleration_across_clocks_and_samples.png with age_acceleration_across_clocks_and_samples.txt.


Effect of condition on age acceleration



Effect of condition on age acceleration


40 comparisons · point and 95% interval · BH-corrected.
Intervals crossing zero are the honest majority. Width tracks sample size, so a wide interval far from zero is a small study, not a large effect.
plot.forest() in Python; written as effect_of_condition_on_age_acceleration.png with effect_of_condition_on_age_acceleration.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Outcomes
Whether acceleration predicts anything that happens to a person.

Survival by age acceleration



Survival by age acceleration


phenoage · 500 subjects · 277 events · log-rank p < 0.001.
Strata are the tails of the acceleration distribution, not a median split: the published figure compares the fastest-ageing tenth with the slowest, because the middle of the distribution is where a clock has least to say. Curves that cross mean the hazard is not proportional, and the hazard ratio beside them is then an average over a period during which the ordering changed.
plot.kaplan_meier() in Python; written as survival_by_age_acceleration.png with survival_by_age_acceleration.txt.


Association with age acceleration



Association with age acceleration


3 tested · 3 pass FDR 0.05.
Effect size against evidence. The dashed line is the Benjamini-Hochberg threshold at the stated FDR, not a raw p-value cut; with thousands of tests the two differ by orders of magnitude. Points far right with small -log10 p are the usual trap: a large effect measured in few samples.
plot.volcano() in Python; written as association_with_age_acceleration.png with association_with_age_acceleration.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
How the clocks relate
Twenty clocks are not twenty measurements. These show how much they share – of their features, and of their answers.

Agreement between clocks



Agreement between clocks


Spearman rank correlation · 53 clocks · 394 samples.
Rank, not Pearson: clocks on different scales have no meaningful linear correlation. Blocks of agreement are usually shared training data.
plot.clock_corr() in Python; written as agreement_between_clocks.png with agreement_between_clocks.txt.


Feature sharing between clocks



Feature sharing between clocks


24 clocks on the ring · 71 pairs sharing at least 5 CpGs.
Chord width is the number of CpGs two clocks have in common. This is the answer to the question the correlation heatmap raises: clocks agree partly because they measure the same biology and partly because they are built from the same probes.
plot.clock_chord() in Python; written as feature_sharing_between_clocks.png with feature_sharing_between_clocks.txt.


Multi-clock profile



Multi-clock profile


12 clocks · 12 groups by condition · z-scored within clock against the cohort.
One closed polygon per group, on a common z scale. A spike on one axis is one clock disagreeing with the rest, which is a finding about the clock at least as often as about the sample.
plot.clock_radar() in Python; written as multi_clock_profile.png with multi_clock_profile.txt.


Samples in clock space



Samples in clock space


PCA of z-scored clock scores · PC1 37% · PC2 21%.
PC1 is almost always chronological age. Structure on PC2 that follows a batch and not a phenotype is a batch effect.
plot.clock_pca() in Python; written as samples_in_clock_space.png with samples_in_clock_space.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Benchmarking
AA1 and AA2 against the ComputAgeBench conditions, and the error-versus-bias tradeoff that decides the ranking.

Datasets detected per clock



Datasets detected per clock


17 clocks · 13 datasets · BH q < 0.05.
AA2 compares cases with their own controls; AA1 tests case-only cohorts against zero. Ordered by the combined total, not by either alone.
plot.benchmark_bars() in Python; written as datasets_detected_per_clock.png with datasets_detected_per_clock.txt.


Error against bias on healthy controls



Error against bias on healthy controls


17 clocks · point size is the benchmark total.
Neither axis is a ranking. A clock at the origin merely predicts chronological age well, which is the one thing a useful clock need not do.
plot.benchmark_error_bias() in Python; written as error_against_bias_on_healthy_controls.png with error_against_bias_on_healthy_controls.txt.


Effect size per clock and dataset



Effect size per clock and dataset


17 clocks x 13 datasets · outlined cells are significant.
Read the columns. A dataset that is blank across every clock is either a condition the clocks cannot see or a cohort too small to show it.
plot.benchmark_heatmap() in Python; written as effect_size_per_clock_and_dataset.png with effect_size_per_clock_and_dataset.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Data quality
Drawn before the results, because a coverage problem invalidates everything after it.

Feature coverage per clock



Feature coverage per clock


8 clocks · floor at 80% · mixed.
The plot to read before the scores. Below the dashed line a clock is mostly scoring imputed values, which is why it was refused.
plot.coverage_bar() in Python; written as feature_coverage_per_clock.png with feature_coverage_per_clock.txt.


Missing values per sample



Missing values per sample


21 samples · median 0.06% missing.
One sample far to the right is a failed array; a shifted whole cohort is a probe filter someone applied upstream.
plot.missingness() in Python; written as missing_values_per_sample.png with missing_values_per_sample.txt.


Beta value distribution per sample



Beta value distribution per sample


27 samples · EPICv1.
Two peaks near 0 and 1 is what a working array looks like. A sample with a filled middle failed, and no downstream normalisation will fix it.
plot.beta_density() in Python; written as beta_value_distribution_per_sample.png with beta_value_distribution_per_sample.txt.


Score distribution by platform



Score distribution by platform


altumage · 3 platforms · 394 samples.
A shift between platforms in the same tissue is a technical effect. It is the reason cross-study comparisons need the platform as a covariate.
plot.platform_comparison() in Python; written as score_distribution_by_platform.png with score_distribution_by_platform.txt.


Score distribution by study



Score distribution by study


altumage · 13 studies · 394 samples.
Between-study spread is usually larger than the within-study effect being tested, which is why AA2 compares cases with their own controls.
plot.study_comparison() in Python; written as score_distribution_by_study.png with score_distribution_by_study.txt.

title: Figure gallery
text:
Other
Figures not yet placed in a section above.

Does the difference hold up across clocks?



Does the difference hold up across clocks?


verdict: unsupported · 44 clocks tested · alpha 0.05.
One bar per clock, coloured by generation; * survives Benjamini-Hochberg and ** survives Bonferroni across the tests actually run. The shape is the finding, not any one bar. A real change lights up across generations; a single lit bar among twenty dark ones is the published signature of a false positive, and five of six re-analysed intervention datasets looked exactly like that.
plot.consensus_plot() in Python; written as does_the_difference_hold_up_across_clocks.png with does_the_difference_hold_up_across_clocks.txt.


How much of each score is the assay



How much of each score is the assay


43 clocks · probe · bar is SE / cohort SD; the label is the raw SE.
Measurement error propagated from published per-probe reliability through each clock’s own weights. The ICC beside each bar is what this cohort implies, not a published figure: green above 0.8, amber below it, red where the assay noise is as large as the spread between these samples, a clock that cannot tell them apart, however confident its point estimate.
plot.reliability_forest() in Python; written as how_much_of_each_score_is_the_assay.png with how_much_of_each_score_is_the_assay.txt.


Scores with the uncertainty they carry



Scores with the uncertainty they carry


dnamphenoage · n = 27 · years.
Two samples whose bars overlap are not distinguishable by this clock on this assay. The narrow bar is measurement error: what a repeat of the same DNA would do. The wide grey bar, where present, is the conformal prediction interval against chronological age, which is a larger question and has a larger answer. Neither is a confidence interval on a diagnosis.
plot.score_interval() in Python; written as scores_with_the_uncertainty_they_carry.png with scores_with_the_uncertainty_they_carry.txt.


What probe loss costs, in years



What probe loss costs, in years


14 clocks · platforms: EPICv1, EPICv2 · measured, not assumed.
Full 450K matrices masked down to each platform’s probe set and rescored, absent probes filled from each clock’s reference values as score() fills them; the bar is the median shift and the whisker a bootstrap interval. A bar at zero is a clock that lost nothing. A long bar is a clock whose lost probes carry weight no fill value stands in for, which is why a correlation check passes while the intercept moves. Reported, never subtracted.
plot.platform_bias() in Python; written as what_probe_loss_costs_in_years.png with what_probe_loss_costs_in_years.txt.

In total
27 figures. Every one is also written per dataset under test/output_figures/<group>/<dataset>/ when the full corpus run is executed; the gallery keeps one representative of each type so a reader does not have to fetch 586 MB to see them.

title: Clinical chemistry and survival
text:
d <- read_clinical("nhanes.csv", units = list(
  albumin = "g/L", creatinine = "umol/L", glucose = "mmol/L", crp = "mg/dL",
  lymphocyte_percent = "%", mean_cell_volume = "fL",
  red_cell_distribution_width = "%", alkaline_phosphatase = "U/L",
  white_blood_cell_count = "10^3/uL", age = "years"))

score(d, clocks = "phenoage")
Units are required and never guessed. Albumin at 4.2 is g/dL and albumin at 42 is g/L; both are clinically normal, and PhenoAge fitted on one returns nonsense for the other. No range check can separate them, so the only correct behaviour is to ask.
KDM and homeostatic dysregulation have no coefficients of their own: each is defined relative to a reference cohort. FALCONAge ships one such fit, BioAge’s NHANES III KDM (fa.models.clinical.kdm_bioage); for any other reference, fit it:
ref <- fit_kdm(nhanes3, markers = markers)
score(d, clocks = "kdm", reference = ref)


LinAge2 (Fong et al. 2025) is trained on survival rather than age: examination, blood and urine inputs in NHANES variable names and units, three scores from health questionnaire items, and a Cox model on principal components, one per sex, returned as the age at which a model on age alone gives the same risk. The inputs are named as in the authors’ codebook, with age and sex in obs:
d = fa.FalconData(X=nhanes_style_inputs, obs=obs[["age", "sex"]], modality="clinical_chemistry")
fa.score(d, clocks=["linage2"])
Cotinine (LBXCOT) in ng/mL is binned into the authors’ four smoking categories. A missing lipid sets LDL to 0, as the authors’ code does, and the result names the samples that happened to; any other missing input leaves that sample without a score. The parameters are what the authors’ linAge2.R fits from the NHANES file it ships with, and FALCONAge reproduces its output to 5e-10 years on the 2,344 subjects of their test wave.



fa.blood_count_ratios(cbc, units={"neutrophils": "10^9/L", "lymphocytes": "10^9/L",
                                  "monocytes": "10^9/L", "platelets": "10^9/L"})
NLR, LMR, PLR and SII from a complete blood count. Units are declared, as everywhere; counts are converted to 10^9/L. Percentages give the two ratios that do not depend on the total (NLR, LMR) and not the two that involve platelets, and a zero lymphocyte count gives no ratio rather than infinity.



A composite clinical clock associated with an outcome does not say which of its markers carries the association. fa.leave_one_marker_out(res, "kdm", data=d, reference=ref, test="outcome") recomputes KDM, HD or PhenoAge without each marker in turn (KDM and HD are refitted; for PhenoAge the marker is held at the reference mean) and reports how far the score and the association moved.

title: Clinical chemistry and survival
text:
Survival and association
Two figures that most aging-clock papers carry, and that need the analysis functions above.

Survival

PythonR


fa.cox_hazard(res, time_col="time", event_col="status")      # HR per unit (per year for an age clock)
fa.plot.kaplan_meier(res, "horvath2013",
                     time_col="time", event_col="status")    # the figure


cox_hazard(res, time_col = "time", event_col = "status")
plot_kaplan_meier(res, "horvath2013", time_col = "time", event_col = "status")



The curves compare the fastest-ageing tenth with the slowest, not two halves. The middle of the acceleration distribution is where a clock discriminates least, so a median split dilutes the comparison; the tails are the published convention. The log-rank p is in the figure’s legend text, the .txt written beside it.
If the curves cross: the hazards are not proportional and the single hazard ratio beside them is an average over a period during which the ordering changed. That is worth saying in a caption rather than leaving for a reader to notice.


Association

PythonR


assoc = fa.associate(res, "crp", covariates=("age", "sex"))
fa.plot.volcano(assoc, fdr=0.05)


assoc <- associate(res, "crp", covariates = c("age", "sex"))
plot_volcano(assoc, fdr = 0.05)



The dashed line is the Benjamini-Hochberg threshold at the stated FDR, read off the q column rather than recomputed. This matters more than it looks: across a few hundred tests a raw 0.05 admits roughly one in twenty of the nulls, and drawing that line instead labels them significant.

title: Uncertainty, specimen and platform
text:
Computing a clock correctly is half the problem. A correctly computed number is still not interpretable on its own, which is what the field’s own literature says and what few implementations do anything about.
Reliability is not a property of a clock alone. The intraclass correlation is 1 - SE^2 / SD^2, so the same technical error divided by a narrower between-sample spread gives a worse coefficient without anything about the assay having changed. A clock with an excellent published ICC, measured on a cohort spanning sixty years of age, can be unable to resolve anything in a trial whose participants are all within a decade of each other. That is the calculation to run before recruiting, not after.

The point estimate problem
Split one DNA sample, run both halves on the same array, and six prominent clocks disagree with themselves by up to nine years (Nat Aging 2022). In adult whole blood many 450K probes are measured unreliably, and the unreliable ones replicate worse (Sugden et al., Patterns 2020;1:100014, doi:10.1016/j.patter.2020.100014). A reader handed “DNAmAge = 54.2” cannot tell whether a 1.5-year change between two draws is biology or the assay.
Every package in the field emits that bare number. FALCONAge emits an interval, and the arithmetic behind it is short enough to check by hand.


Propagating measurement error
A linear clock is score = f(b + wᵀβ). Give each probe a measurement variance σ²ⱼ and the score’s variance follows directly:
\[\operatorname{Var} = f'(\text{raw})^2 \sum_j w_j^2\,\sigma_j^2\]
\[\sigma_j^2 = s_j^2\,(1 - \mathrm{ICC}_j)\]
with s²ⱼ the spread of probe j across the cohort in front of you and ICCⱼ its published test-retest reliability. One matrix–vector product per clock.
Three parts of that are load-bearing:
The ICC table is measured, not assumed. registry/data/probe_icc.csv.gz carries 283,860 probes, derived from 69 blood samples each assayed twice on EPIC v1 and preprocessed with SeSAMe 2, using the two-way random-effects, absolute-agreement, single-rating model, ICC(2,1) (Epigenetics 2024, CC BY 4.0). Its citation, licence and SHA-256 go into the run manifest, because an interval whose provenance is not recorded is worse than no interval.
An imputed feature contributes its full variance. Not the reduced s²(1−ICC). An imputed probe is the cohort mean or a published reference; it carries no information about the sample in front of you. Treating it as well-measured would make worse data produce a narrower interval, which is the wrong direction and the part of the calculation most likely to look like a bug.
The output transform is differentiated, not linearised once. Horvath’s anti_log_linear has slope 21·eˣ below zero and 21 above it, so a child’s uncertainty and an adult’s scale differently from the same raw error. Every op in the catalogue has an analytic derivative; the four that destroy the information (binarize, rank_normalize, quantile_normalize, simplex_projection) have none, and a chain containing one refuses rather than skipping the step and returning a confidently small interval.
The sum assumes probe errors are independent, and they are not. Writing \(\sum_j w_j^2 \sigma_j^2\) drops the cross term \(2\sum_{j<k} w_j w_k \operatorname{Cov}(\varepsilon_j, \varepsilon_k)\). Chip position, plate and scanner drift move many probes together, and those covariances are positive far more often than negative, so the SE reported here is a lower bound, and not necessarily a tight one, since a clock with hundreds of positively correlated terms can have a true SE several times this.
The honest alternative does not exist: a \(319{,}607 \times 319{,}607\) error covariance would need replicate designs nobody publishes. What exists is a cross-check. source="clock" derives the same quantity from a published clock-level ICC measured on real technical replicates, which does contain the correlated part; when the two disagree substantially, the clock-level figure is the one to believe and the gap is the correlated component the probe path cannot see. icc_from_replicates() closes it properly on your own duplicates. This is stated rather than buried because an interval presented without its assumption is exactly the false precision the section exists to argue against.
On the corpus, Horvath 2013 comes out at ±1.58 years of technical error with an implied cohort ICC of 0.98; DunedinPoAm38 is the least repeatable at 0.72; the 319,607-probe BLUP clock reaches 1.00, because a weight spread thinly over the whole array averages the noise away. Read all three as lower bounds, for the reason just given.


Prediction error is a different, larger question
technical_se() asks what a repeat of the same DNA would do. conformal_interval() asks how far the number is from the truth.
Split conformal: take healthy whole-blood samples with known ages, compute the absolute residuals, and the ⌈(n+1)(1−α)⌉/n quantile is a half-width that covers the truth at the stated rate on any exchangeable sample. No distributional assumption is made, and the guarantee is finite-sample. Conformalised quantile regression (Genet Epidemiol 2025) is the better version, widening the interval where the training data were sparse; it needs fitted quantile models, so split conformal ships and the calibration table reports the width per age band so a reader can see where one width is lying.
The calibration takes whole blood, buffy coat and peripheral blood leukocytes from adults, and nothing else. The corpus also labels sorted populations and PBMC as blood, and on those a whole-blood clock’s residual carries the cell type: on its healthy controls Hannum ran 21 years low on CD8+ T cells, and DNAm PhenoAge 24 years low on CD14+ monocytes and 40 on CD8+ T cells. Until that was noticed they were more than half the calibration set, and the widths quoted composition as clock error.
The limitation is not small and is stated in the output: every row carries exchangeable = False. The calibration cohort is adult, blood, and overwhelmingly of European ancestry. On a paediatric or non-European cohort the guarantee does not transfer, and no widening factor would make it.


What the calibration found, and what it turned into
The first calibration put Ying’s DamAge and AdaptAge 37–150 years from chronological age. The obvious reading (“these are not age predictors”) turned out to be wrong, and the measurement that settled it is worth reproducing because the distinction it draws is a general one.
Regress predicted on chronological across the corpus’s healthy cohorts:

DamAge’s slope is 0.967, better than DNAmPhenoAge’s 1.199. It tracks age. What it does not have is a fixed origin: its offset against chronological age is −84 years in one healthy cohort and +78 in another.
The mechanism is visible in one number. DamAge and AdaptAge move as near mirror images, r = −0.975 across datasets, and the swing in their sum is only 33 years against 162 for each alone. Their published intercepts are +543.43 and −511.97; a dataset-level shift in overall methylation pushes one up and the other down by nearly the same amount. One shared offset, hugely amplified, not two broken clocks.
So neither obvious label fits. age_years would license predicted − chronological, which measures the cohort. relative_score would forbid the residual and the group difference, the operations the paper itself reports, and would contradict a unit of years and a training target of chronological age, both of which are accurate.
They are age_years_relative: years, slope near one, no fixed zero. LEGAL_OPS admits residual, difference, mean and correlate, and refuses acceleration. The vocabulary had listed acceleration and residual separately since v1.0 and nothing had ever read the difference; this is the first clock that needs it.


Specimen type is not metadata
Same 91 people, three specimens (bioRxiv 2025.09.16.673560, CATSLife1, mean age 30.9):



Comparison
Mean difference in clock age
Spearman between the two




saliva vs buffy coat
3.83 – 16.46 years
0.45 – 0.69


saliva vs PBMC
in the same direction
0.25 – 0.55


buffy coat vs PBMC
−0.06 – 0.39 years
0.66 – 0.87



Read the two columns together, because separately each is reassuring. Saliva and buffy coat clock ages correlate at up to 0.69, a correlation most people would accept, and are still a decade apart. Correlation is not agreement, and the check that gets run is the correlation. The blood pair is the control: same study, same pipeline, difference under half a year, which is what makes the saliva number a specimen effect rather than noise.
Which clock matters as much as which specimen. On those samples a pace-of-aging clock differed by −0.007 biological years per chronological year (p = 0.486) where Hannum differed by 12.5 years, so “this clock transfers” is a per-clock fact, not a per-tissue one, and FALCONAge therefore holds the policy per clock. Across unrelated tissues the published figure is 20–30 years (PMC12714307).
FALCONAge reads obs["tissue"] against each clock’s declared training tissue and takes one of three positions:

allow

the genuinely pan-tissue clocks. Nothing to say.

warn

the default. Says what the clock was fitted on, what it was given, and the measured discordance where one is published.

refuse

twelve clocks whose training tissue has no counterpart elsewhere: four placenta clocks, three cord-blood clocks, neonatal blood spots, buccal, and three brain clocks. A placenta clock on blood is a category error, not an offset.


Not every package holds a policy. methylclock 1.16.0’s DNAmAge() takes no tissue argument and, with its default clocks = "all", returns PedBE, a buccal clock (McEwen et al., PNAS 2020), for blood. FALCONAge refuses PedBE on blood, so a clock missing from a FALCONAge run that another package reported is sometimes the refusal working.
Cell-free DNA is refused by every clock regardless of policy. It is not a tissue a clock generalises to; it is a fragment population shed from many of them, and array clocks applied to it directly perform poorly (bioRxiv 2025.11.27.690895).
And when obs has no tissue column at all, the run says so once, because silence was the previous behaviour, and silence is the bug.






NoteThis check found a real error in our own test suite



At first the integration tests scored the three Lee placenta clocks on GSE66459, which is umbilical cord blood, and asserted only that the answers looked like gestational weeks. They did, because gestational age is gestational age whatever tissue you read it from. That is exactly the failure the check exists to catch, and it caught it here first.




Probe loss, priced
probe_loss() has always said how much of a model is absent: count and coefficient mass. It could not say what that costs. Now it can, because the cost was measured: every full-450K matrix in the corpus, masked down to each platform’s probe set and rescored, 206 samples across eight datasets. The two right-hand columns are the same masks under two ways of filling an absent CpG: the mean of the clock’s present CpGs in the data, which FALCONAge used until the reference values existed, and the clock’s reference value, which it uses now.

Most of what the pooled column prices is the fill, not the loss. A pooled value sits near 0.5, and clock CpGs are often near 0 or 1: lin lost three probes of ninety-nine and moved nine years. Filled from the reference, the same masks move hannum, lin, hrsinchphenoage and yingdamage by about a year or less; over the 19 rows on the years scale whose fill changed, the median absolute shift fell from 3.36 to 0.66 years, and 38 of the 45 rows with a reference moved less. Those numbers are out of sample: the blood reference is a mean over healthy controls in this corpus, so each dataset was scored against it rebuilt without that dataset (scored in-sample, hannum read −0.40 rather than +1.03). yingcausage still moves six years, its 93 lost CpGs carrying weight that no fixed value stands in for.
zhangblup fills nothing, because an absent probe drops out after the per-sample standardisation, and loses ten percent of a 319,607-probe model for under half a year at the median, a graceful degradation. Its shift has two parts. Scored on the same samples, the lost probes alone move the estimate by −0.64 y at the median, and restandardising over the EPIC v2 probe set by +0.15 y. And the two rows at exactly zero are the internal check: a clock that loses nothing must shift by nothing, and does.
What the table does not cover, so it is not read as covering it. 86 rows: 43 clocks × two targets, EPIC v1 and EPIC v2. For the six deconvolution entries the shift is not probe loss alone: a 450K matrix is deconvolved with the 350-CpG legacy IDOL table and an EPIC one with the 450-CpG table, so their rows price a change of array, which is what a user moving between arrays sees (a median shift of at most 0.034 in a cell-type proportion). 450K is the reference the shift is measured from, so it cannot appear, its shift is zero by construction, not by measurement. 27K is absent for a different reason: masking a 450K matrix to 27,578 probes leaves most of these clocks below the coverage floor, so what would be measured is the shift of a clock that would have been refused anyway. And the reference cohort is 206 blood-derived samples of adults, whole blood and leukocytes as well as PBMC and sorted T cells; a shift measured there is a reasonable prior for another blood cohort and not a correction factor for a different tissue.
The shift is reported and never applied. An automatic offset would be a second number nobody can trace, which is the failure the coefficient digests exist to prevent.
Platform loss or probe QC. A clock CpG can be absent for two reasons, and only one of them is permanent. If the array does not carry it, nothing recovers it. If the array carries it and the data lacks it, it was measured and then removed, almost always by probe filters (SNP-affected, cross-reactive, failed detection) that belong to an epigenome-wide association study and not to clock scoring. A table bundled with the package records which arrays (27K, 450K, EPIC v1, EPIC v2) carry each clock CpG, built from the Illumina manifests and, for EPIC v2, the Zhou lab InfiniumAnnotation manifest. With it, probe_loss() counts the second kind in n_removed_by_qc and qc_removed_mass, and score() warns (category probe_qc) once the removed CpGs carry 1% of a clock’s |coefficient|. Nothing is downloaded during scoring. On QC-filtered betas this separates CpGs removed by a filter from CpGs the array never carried, and for a clock such as DNAmTL the first kind can be most of what is missing. The remedy is to score clocks on normalised but unfiltered betas.


Before the first array, and after the last
power() answers “how many samples to see this effect on this clock”, and needs no data file. It refuses to default the standard deviation, because n scales with its square and a guessed SD is a guessed answer reported to three significant figures. Where a reliability figure is available it splits the answer: at ICC 0.9, a tenth of the sample size exists only to average out the instrument. That is the arithmetic behind the published finding that the original clocks need 3 to 16 replicates per condition where more reliable versions need 1 to 2.
consensus() implements the decision rule from When to Trust Epigenetic Clocks [77]. Re-analysing six intervention datasets, the authors found that in five of six exactly one clock reached significance, a first-generation clock every time, and four of those five lost it under multiple-testing correction. Their conclusion, in their words: a single significant clock after an intervention is likely a false positive. The same group later widened this to 16 clocks and 94 further biomarkers across the 51 longitudinal studies of TranslAGE [78], which is where the clock grouping the FALCONAge report uses comes from.
So consensus() tests every scored clock, corrects across the whole set actually run, and returns a verdict rather than a table to pick from: supported needs significance across at least two generations including an outcome-trained clock and survival of Bonferroni; one lit clock is unsupported whatever its p-value. The verdict string always carries the counts it was computed from, a verdict without its arithmetic is an oracle, and that is the opposite of the posture of this package.
Repeated measures. An intervention usually measures the same people more than once, and treating each visit as a new person lets the spread between people swamp the change within them. design="paired" tests each person’s change from one visit to another (subject_col names the person); design="mixed" fits y ~ visit + (1 | person) by REML, keeps a person who missed a visit, and takes any number of visits, testing them jointly. It reproduces nlme::lme on a design with missing visits: estimates to 1e-7, standard errors to 1e-6, and the containment degrees of freedom exactly (Pinheiro & Bates 2000). Both add mdc95, the minimum detectable change 1.96·√2·SEM with the SEM the within-person SD across the visits (Weir 2005), and flag a significant mean change that is smaller than it: twelve people can make a group change of 1.6 SD of the change significant while no one of them could be shown to have changed. That SEM holds day-to-day biology and assay noise together; technical_se() gives the assay part alone, and variance_components() separates the two when there are technical replicates.


Evidence, attached to the score
result.evidence() returns what a value on this clock has been shown to predict, with effect sizes and DOIs. Seeded from studies that tested many clocks on one cohort under one protocol, so the rows are comparable to each other, such as the observation that first-generation clocks account for about 5 % of significant disease associations across 174 outcomes in 18,859 people (Nat Commun 2025).
A row without a DOI is rejected at load time. An uncheckable effect size looks identical to a checkable one in a table, and is worth less than nothing.
The most useful row is not about any clock. Across 39 biomarkers in more than 20,000 people, a clock’s chronological-age accuracy and its mortality prediction are uncorrelated: R = 0.12, P = 0.67 (Nat Aging 2025). That is the empirical justification for scale_type and LEGAL_OPS, and it is the reason “which clock is most accurate” is the wrong question.


What was deliberately not built
Recorded so it does not appear by accident.

No silent correction. Batch reference, platform offset and interval are all reported. A score adjusted by an untraceable factor destroys the provenance discipline that is the reason to use this package.
No percentile against an unnamed population. The same person reads as accelerated or decelerated depending on the comparator; a percentile without a cited reference cohort means different things to different readers.
No diagnostic thresholds. None exist in the literature. Nothing here is coloured red above a cut-off.
No LLM dependency. A scoring library whose output depends on a model that changes weekly is not reproducible.

title: 23. Building a clock of your own
text: The catalogue is other people’s clocks. This is the arithmetic of fitting one, with the numbers the published clocks actually used.

title: 23. Building a clock of your own
text:
The objective
With \(n\) samples and \(p\) CpGs, \(p \gg n\) always. Horvath had 8,000 samples against 21,369 candidate probes; a modern EPIC study has 850,000 columns and a few hundred rows. An unpenalised least-squares fit is not identifiable, because \(X^\top X\) is singular whenever \(p > n\). Penalisation is what makes the problem have an answer, not a refinement on one.
\[
\hat{\beta} = \arg\min_{\beta} \left\{ \frac{1}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - x_i^{\top}\beta\right)^2 + \lambda\left[\frac{1-\alpha}{2}\lVert\beta\rVert_2^2 + \alpha\lVert\beta\rVert_1\right] \right\}
\]
The two penalties do different work. The \(\ell_1\) term has a corner at zero, so its subgradient can hold a coefficient exactly at zero, which is what performs selection. The \(\ell_2\) term is smooth and shrinks correlated predictors together rather than choosing between them, which matters because neighbouring CpGs are strongly correlated and pure LASSO picks among them close to arbitrarily.









\(\alpha\)
Name
Behaviour on correlated CpGs
Used by




1
LASSO
Selects one per correlated group, close to arbitrarily
eFRS, the McCartney EpiScores


0.5
Elastic net
Keeps correlated groups together while still zeroing most coefficients
Horvath 2013


0
Ridge
Shrinks everything, selects nothing
Rarely used alone



Horvath fitted \(\alpha = 0.5\) with \(\lambda = 0.0226\) chosen by cross-validation, over the 21,369 probes shared by the 27K and 450K platforms that had fewer than ten missing values. That produced the 353 sites.






ImportantThe selected set is not the biology



Rerun the same fit with a slightly different \(\lambda\), a different fold split, or a different subset of samples, and a different CpG set comes out with almost identical accuracy. The correlated groups are interchangeable to the optimiser. This is one mechanism behind the discrepancies listed in section Where the paper and the coefficients disagree, and it is why two faithful implementations of the same clock can disagree on membership.

title: 23. Building a clock of your own
text:
Choosing the penalty honestly
\(\lambda\) comes from \(k\)-fold cross-validation: fit on \(k-1\) folds, measure on the held-out one, take the \(\lambda\) minimising mean cross-validated error, or the largest \(\lambda\) within one standard error of it for a sparser model.
Any step that looked at the outcome must sit inside the loop. Selecting CpGs by their correlation with age on the full dataset and then cross-validating the fit on those CpGs leaks the held-out fold into the selection, and the reported error is optimistic by an amount that cannot be recovered afterwards.

title: 23. Building a clock of your own
text:
The age transform
Methylation changes quickly in childhood and slowly afterwards, so a model linear in age fits adults and misses the first two decades. Horvath regresses a transformed age and inverts afterwards, with \(A = 20\). Up to \(A\),
\[
F(\text{age}) = \log(\text{age} + 1) - \log(A + 1),
\]
and above it,
\[
F(\text{age}) = \frac{\text{age} - A}{A + 1}.
\]
Both branches give 0 at \(\text{age} = A\) and both have derivative \(1/(A+1)\) there, so \(F\) is continuous and differentiable at the join. The model predicts \(F\); the reported age is \(F^{-1}\) of the linear predictor. Applying the inverse twice, or omitting it, is invisible in an adult cohort because the branches nearly agree there, and badly wrong in a paediatric one.

text:
Feature selection is not settled
Elastic net is the default rather than the optimum. Benchmarked on the Hannum blood data (GSE40279, 656 samples, 473,035 CpGs, 10-fold cross-validation, 80/20 split) by Li et al. 2022 (doi:10.1371/journal.pcbi.1009938):
