title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Every clock in the catalogue models the mean beta at a set of sites and returns one number. That is not the only thing a methylation matrix can be asked, and on the field’s own evidence it may not be the most informative thing.
Tong et al. [65] quantified how much of a clock is entropy rather than biology: roughly 66 to 75 per cent of Horvath2013’s accuracy against chronological age is reproducible by a purely stochastic model of methylation change, about 90 per cent for Zhang, and about 63 per cent for PhenoAge. The gradient is the interesting part. The more accurately a clock predicts chronological age, the more of it is drift.
This page covers five things FALCONAge computes that are not clocks: the disorder readouts, repertoire structure, where a clock’s coefficient mass sits, reliability components, and mosaic ages within a tissue. None of them returns an age, none is gated by scale_type, and none is comparable between datasets processed differently.

title: Beyond the clock score
section: Disorder: entropy, drift and the barometer
text:
Disorder: entropy, drift and the barometer
falconage.disorder holds four functions, and the division between them is about what carries the number, which is the distinction most easily lost.








Function
Returns
Per what




fa.entropy
how far the methylome sits from fully committed
sample


fa.drift
how far a sample sits from the cohort centroid
sample


fa.noise_barometer
summed per-site SD over age-variable sites
group


fa.variable_sites
which cytosines widen with age
site




Entropy
Normalised Shannon entropy over the beta matrix:
\[
S = \frac{1}{N \log \tfrac{1}{2}} \sum_{i=1}^{N}
    \Big[ \beta_i \log \beta_i + (1-\beta_i) \log (1-\beta_i) \Big]
\]
Bounded 0 to 1. A site at beta 0 or 1 is decided and contributes nothing; a site at 0.5 is maximally uncertain and contributes its full share. So \(S = 0\) is a methylome where every site is committed and \(S = 1\) is one where none of them is.
import falconage as fa

data = fa.read("betas.csv")
ent = fa.entropy(data)        # entropy, n_sites
n_sites is not decoration. Entropy is a mean over sites, so a mean over different sites is not a comparison. The default restricts to sites covered in every sample for exactly that reason; set complete_sites=False to use each sample’s own coverage and then read n_sites before comparing any two rows.
On the test corpus this lands at 0.695 with an SD of 0.007 across 825,177 complete sites, which is what a clean bimodal EPIC distribution looks like once it is summarised to one number.


Drift
The barometer is a property of a group, which leaves nothing to regress against an outcome. fa.drift is the per-sample analogue: the distance from the cohort centroid, computed leave-one-out so that a sample is never scored against a mean it helped compute.
dri = fa.drift(data)                          # drift from this cohort
dri = fa.drift(data, reference=young_mean)    # drift from a young reference
The leave-one-out default matters more than it looks. Scoring a sample against a centroid that includes it shrinks its own distance, and in a small cohort that shrinkage is large enough to invert a group difference.


Which sites actually widen
The barometer of Mei et al. [70] is defined over “cytosines whose variance rises with age”, and that clause is the whole statistic. Summed over every site instead, the sum is dominated by sites that are merely variable, most of which have nothing to do with age.
fa.variable_sites is that selection step, split out so it can be inspected rather than assumed. The test is Brown-Forsythe, which is Levene’s test using the median, across age bins. Bartlett’s test is the more common choice in this literature and is the wrong one here: it assumes normality within each group, and beta values near 0 or 1 are visibly not normal, so Bartlett reports variance differences that are distributional artefacts.
A significant result says the variances differ between bins. It does not say variance rises, and a site whose variance falls is just as significant, so direction carries the sign of the trend and rising is the conjunction the barometer wants.






ImportantWhat this looks like on a cohort that is too small



Run on the test corpus, sites_rising under Benjamini-Hochberg is zero. Twenty-seven samples in three bins of nine, against roughly 820,000 tests, has almost no power once the correction is applied.
That is the correct answer, not a gap in the implementation. A barometer that means anything needs a cohort in the hundreds. fa.noise_barometer accepts an explicit sites= list so a selection made elsewhere can be reused, which is also the only way the statistic transfers between cohorts.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Repertoire structure
falconage.immune addresses a covariate no published blood clock carries.
Deconvolution answers how many cells of each type. It says nothing about how many distinct clones those cells represent, and the two are different measurements: two donors with an identical CD8 memory fraction can differ by orders of magnitude in clone count.

Why clone count should move a clock at all
Take one cell type holding fraction \(f\) of the sample, split into clones of relative size \(w_k\) with \(\sum_k w_k = 1\). Give clone \(k\) a somatic offset \(\delta_k\) from its lineage mean at some site, with mean zero and variance \(\sigma^2\). The compartment’s bulk beta is the size-weighted mean, so
\[
\mathrm{Var}\Big[\sum_k w_k \delta_k\Big] = \sigma^2 \sum_k w_k^2
   = \frac{\sigma^2}{N_{\text{eff}}},
\qquad N_{\text{eff}} = \Big(\sum_k w_k^2\Big)^{-1}
\]
and \(\sum_k w_k^2\) is exactly the Simpson index. The variance a clonal compartment contributes to bulk methylation is inversely proportional to its effective number of clones, and clone count enters through that quantity and no other. Three equal clones carry one cell’s somatic state at full weight; ten thousand clones average it to nothing.
This is why the effect is invisible to composition adjustment: \(f\) can be identical between two donors while \(N_{\text{eff}}\) differs thousand-fold, and every published blood clock sees only \(f\).
The myeloid version of the question is settled. Nachun et al. [71] measured clonal hematopoiesis against six clocks and found 1.31 years of acceleration on GrimAge to 3.08 on extrinsic EEAA. The lymphoid analogue has not been asked.


Measuring it
div = fa.repertoire_diversity(clones, sample_col="sample_id", count_col="count")
data.obs = data.obs.join(div)

res = fa.score(data, clocks="compatible")
acc = fa.acceleration(res, adjust=["clonality", "cd8mem_fraction"])
fa.acceleration already accepts arbitrary obs columns as covariates, so the incremental test is one call. The question is entirely whether clonality adds variance beyond cell fraction.
Depth is the trap. Richness and Shannon both rise with sequencing depth, so an unrarefied comparison between a deeply and a shallowly sequenced donor measures the library rather than the donor. Pass rarefy="min" to subsample every donor to a common depth by multivariate hypergeometric draw, which is what a shallower run would actually have produced; sampling with replacement inflates richness at low depth, in the same direction as the bias being corrected. clonality, simpson and effective_clones are far more stable and are the ones to trust when rarefaction is not possible.


Simulating it
The mechanism arm needs no paired cohort. fa.simulate_clonality generates bulk methylomes at fixed cell fractions and varying clone structure, so anything a clock does in response is clone structure alone.
sim = fa.simulate_clonality(
    reference, {"CD8mem": 0.3, "Neu": 0.7},
    clonal_types=["CD8mem"],
    clone_sizes=[fa.immune.zipf_clone_sizes(n, alpha=1.0)
                 for n in (2, 20, 200, 2000)],
    n_replicates=20)
res = fa.score(sim, clocks="compatible")
reference is sorted-cell mean beta, features by cell type. The six-cell IDOL library that the bundled deconvolution entries use (FlowSorted.Blood.EPIC, GPL-3) is one such table: fa.registry.load().deconvolution_table("deconvolutebloodepicbcell", "EPICv1") returns it, 450 CpGs by six cell types.






NoteWhat the simulation returns on the test corpus



Across 42 clocks scored on 48 simulated samples at identical cell fractions, the median log-log slope of score spread against effective clone count is -0.494, interquartile range -0.559 to -0.415. The derivation predicts -0.5 and was not fitted to the simulation.
Among the clocks reporting years, dnamphenoage moves 4.35 years between an effectively-two-clone compartment and a diverse one, and horvath2013 moves 1.54 years. Both fall below a year once the compartment holds a few hundred effective clones.
Cell-type fractions were identical for every one of those samples, so composition adjustment cannot remove any of it.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Where a clock’s weight sits
A clock is a weight vector over CpGs, and two questions about that vector need no samples at all.
Is this clock exposed to genotype? If a clock CpG is under strong meQTL control and the allele frequency at that variant differs between ancestral populations, a systematic difference in clock output between ancestry groups follows from genotype frequency alone, with no difference in aging. Cruz-Gonzalez et al. [75] established that the major clocks lose accuracy in admixed individuals; whether the size of that loss tracks each clock’s meQTL exposure is open, and half of that measurement is a property of the coefficients.
Is this clock regulatory? Patel et al. [76] report that most CpGs used by established clocks do not overlap known transcription factor binding sites. Reproducing that against any annotation class is the same computation with a different list.
mass = fa.coefficient_mass({"meqtl": godmc_cpgs, "enhancer": enhancer_cpgs})

Why mass and not count
Counting annotated sites answers the wrong question. A clock’s behaviour is driven by its heavy features: a 353-CpG clock with two enormous weights and 351 small ones behaves like a two-CpG clock. The statistic is therefore the share of \(\sum_j |w_j|\) on annotated sites, with the plain count returned beside it. When the two diverge, the annotated sites are the heavy ones, and that divergence is the finding.
Run on the registry with each clock’s own CpG set as the annotation, which needs no external file, horvath2013 shares 11.6 per cent of its sites with dnamphenoage but 19.6 per cent of its mass. weidner shares two of its three sites with dnamphenoage and 89 per cent of its mass. Two clocks that share their heaviest features will agree with each other for reasons that have nothing to do with either being right.
FALCONAge bundles no annotation list. meQTL catalogues and regulatory builds are large, versioned and separately licensed, and freezing one into a wheel would make it silently stale. GoDMC and the EPIGEN meQTL database are the usual sources for the first question, the Ensembl Regulatory Build or a Roadmap chromatin-state track for the second. .attrs["unmatched"] reports how many supplied ids matched nothing, which is the check that catches an EPIC v2 list with _TC21 suffixes meeting bare cg probe ids.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Reliability: trait, state and technical
A published ICC answers “how reproducible is this clock across a cohort”. Someone asking “has my number moved” needs a different quantity, and the gap between the two is why clock ICCs in the literature read as reassuring while replicate disagreement of up to nine years is also true [68].
fa.variance_components separates them, given repeated measurement:
\[
y_{ijk} = \mu + a_i + s_{ij} + \varepsilon_{ijk}
\]
for person \(i\), occasion \(j\), replicate \(k\), fitted by Henderson’s method of moments. Two ICCs come back and the gap between them is the point:

icc

On raw scores. Comparable to what the literature publishes.

icc_age_adjusted

The same after chronological age is regressed out. A cohort spanning decades holds most of its between-person variance in the age term, so a raw ICC largely reports that the clock tracks age, which was never in question. The adjusted figure is between-person reliability among people of the same age, which is what any individual-level claim rests on.


A clock whose raw ICC is 0.98 and whose adjusted ICC is 0.4 is not a precise instrument. It is a cohort with a wide age range.
vc = fa.variance_components(res, subject_col="donor", occasion_col="visit")
vc.table                      # var_trait, var_state, var_tech, icc, icc_age_adjusted
vc.replicates_needed(0.9)     # per occasion, to reach ICC 0.9
With one draw per visit and no technical replicates, which is the usual longitudinal design, day-to-day change and assay noise cannot be told apart: var_state then holds both, var_tech is NaN, icc is the test-retest reliability across visits, and vc.design["within_person"] says so.
replicates_needed returns inf where no number of replicates gets there, and that is the informative case rather than an error. Replicates average away the technical term only, so a clock whose day-to-day within-person variance already exceeds the budget cannot be rescued by running the array again. The honest answer is then a second draw, not a second scan.
Components are not clipped at zero. A negative one means the within-level spread exceeded the between-level spread, which is real for a small design or a clock measuring nothing in this cohort, and rounding it to zero disguises both.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
Mosaic ages within a tissue
fa.models.single_cell.scage gives an age per cell [28]. A bulk clock already reports the mean, so the quantity worth having is the shape of the distribution underneath it: a tissue whose cells are uniformly middle-aged and one holding a mixture of young and very old cells have the same bulk methylation and, plausibly, very different biology.
The obstacle is that single-cell methylation coverage is sparse, so each per-cell age rests on few sites and carries large error. Observed spread is therefore always positive, and reporting it as heterogeneity is the mistake fa.mosaic exists to avoid.
The null is stated plainly: every cell in the group has the same true age, and all observed spread is estimation error. It is simulated by drawing each cell from a normal centred on the group mean with that cell’s own standard error, taken from the profile-likelihood width scage already returns.
ages = fa.models.single_cell.scage(cells, reference)
mos  = fa.mosaic(ages, group="tissue")
A small p_excess is evidence of genuine mosaicism. A large one says the data cannot distinguish a mosaic tissue from a uniform one measured badly, which at typical single-cell coverage is the usual answer and is worth reporting as such. n_at_grid_edge counts cells whose estimate landed on the boundary of the age grid, where the likelihood was truncated rather than maximised; those pile up and inflate the tails, so a group with many of them should have its skew and kurtosis ignored.

title: Beyond the clock score
text:
What none of this is
None of these functions is a clock, and none returns an age. They carry no coefficients, no scale_type gate applies, and their outputs move with normalisation, probe panel and detection-p filtering. The only defensible comparison is within one processed matrix.
That is a real constraint rather than a disclaimer. Entropy computed on noob-normalised betas and entropy computed on raw betas are different numbers for the same DNA, and neither is more correct than the other.

title: Uncertainty, specimen and platform
text:
Technical replicates of the same DNA differ by up to nine years on prominent clocks, so a bare number does not say whether a difference between two samples is real.

PythonR


se = fa.technical_se(res, d)
se.diagnostics[["median_se", "se_over_sd", "implied_cohort_icc"]]

fa.conformal_interval(res, level=0.90)     # the other, larger uncertainty
fa.power("horvath2013", effect=0.5, result=res)   # how many samples you need


u <- technical_se(res, d)
u$diagnostics

conformal_interval(res, level = 0.90)
power_n("horvath2013", effect = 0.5, result = res)




              method  n_features  median_se  se_over_sd  implied_cohort_icc
horvath2013    probe         353       1.58        0.14                0.98
hannum         probe          71       2.46        0.22                0.95
dunedinpoam38  probe          46       0.04        0.53                0.72

Two samples whose intervals overlap are not distinguishable by that clock on that assay, however different their point estimates look.
→ Why it works this way: Uncertainty, specimen and platform

title: Loading your data
text:
FALCONAge scores data that is already preprocessed and quality controlled. Normalisation, detection filtering and sample QC of methylation arrays belong upstream, in an array pipeline such as methylarray, minfi or SeSAMe; FALCONAge takes their beta matrix as input. Clinical chemistry and NMR tables are read as reported by the laboratory.
Every reader returns a FalconData: a samples-by-features matrix with its modality, platform and sample annotation. Scoring is the same call whichever reader produced it.
Every output on this page was produced by running the code above it, against the public test corpus where the corpus has that input type and against a small file written inline where it does not. Nothing here is illustrative.

fa.read(path) selects the reader from the file name. Arguments specific to a reader, such as the units of a clinical table, are passed to that reader directly.

title: Loading your data
text:
A beta matrix
Probes down the rows, samples across the columns, or the transpose: the orientation is detected from which axis carries probe ids.
d = fa.read_betas("betas.csv")
FalconData(3 samples x 3 features, dna_methylation, 0.0% missing)
The file that produced it:
probe,S001,S002,S003
cg00000029,0.512,0.488,0.559
cg00000165,0.113,0.096,0.140
cg00000236,0.842,0.871,0.836
Betas belong in 0 to 1. A matrix of percentages is a factor of a hundred out and every clock will return a confidently wrong number, so prepare() checks the range and says so.
EPIC v2 identifiers are harmonised automatically. EPIC v2 probe ids carry a suffix (cg00000029_TC21), and a clock fitted on 450K finds no matching features until the suffixes are removed. prepare() removes them and averages replicate probes of the same CpG; aggregate_epicv2=False disables the step.
Pass the matrix before probe filtering. Filters for SNP, cross-reactive or detection-failed probes are designed for association studies. A clock CpG removed by them is replaced by an imputed value at scoring time, and score() reports how much of each clock’s weight that affects (see Preparing data and coverage).

C01           55.79
C02           69.61
Units are per column, not per file. A clinical table mixes them, so there is no single name to pass; units="SI" is refused with the mapping it wants. PhenoAge exists in an SI and a conventional variant that disagree by years, and units= has no default for that reason.
HbA1c in mmol/mol. Laboratories outside the US report HbA1c in IFCC units. Declare "hba1c": "mmol/mol" and it is converted to the NGSP percentage the reference models were fitted in, by the published master equation NGSP = 0.09148 × IFCC + 2.152 (NGSP; Hoelzel et al., Clin Chem 2004;50:166-174, doi:10.1373/clinchem.2003.024802). It is not a ratio, so it applies to HbA1c only.
A cohort measured unlike its reference. KDM and homeostatic dysregulation are fitted on a reference cohort, and fit_kdm/fit_hd record each marker’s distribution there. When a scored cohort leaves it, score() says so (category reference_range): a median outside the reference’s 1st to 99th percentile, which is what a unit mismatch looks like, or many values beyond the reference’s range. The case that matters most is CRP. NHANES III’s assay read nothing below 0.21 mg/dL, and 63.9% of its adults sit at that floor, so a high-sensitivity CRP cohort scored against it has most of its values where the reference has none. fa.models.clinical.censor_to_reference(df, ref) sets values below a reference’s reporting floor to the floor, which is how the reference itself recorded them, and returns how many moved. It only touches markers whose minimum is a floor (at least 1% of reference rows sitting exactly at it); values above the reference’s range are real measurements and are left alone.

title: Loading your data
text:
NMR metabolomics
A Nightingale Health export (CSV, TSV or Excel), samples down the rows:
d = fa.read_nightingale("nightingale.xlsx")      # Excel needs the `metabolomics` extra (openpyxl)
res = fa.score(d, clocks=["metaboage", "metabohealth"])
Column names are translated to the BBMRI-NL names the two scores were fitted with, by MiMIR’s table and MiMIR’s rule (lower-cased, and translated only when exactly one entry lists the name); a name the table does not know is kept and listed in obs.attrs["untranslated"] rather than guessed. MetaboAge (van den Akker et al. 2020) and MetaboHealth (Deelen et al. 2019) are scored as MiMIR scores them, its quality control included, and match it to 1e-9 and 1e-12. MetaboHealth z-scores each measure within the cohort, so a score depends on who else is in the file: it is marked requires_cohort and is not comparable between files scored separately.

title: Loading your data
text:
After loading
Whatever you loaded, the rest is the same:
res = fa.score(d, clocks="compatible")   # only the clocks this data supports
res.interpretation()                     # scale, unit, legal operations, caveats
fa.technical_se(res, d)                  # how much of each score is the assay
clocks="compatible" is the safe default: it asks the registry which clocks this platform, modality and specimen actually support, and skips the rest by name rather than scoring them on whatever features happen to match.

title: About and design
text:
FALCONAge computes biological age scores from molecular data. It reads what a laboratory actually produces, applies published aging clocks to it, and returns each score with its unit, its provenance, and an estimate of how much of it is measurement noise.
An aging clock is a supervised model mapping molecular features, most often DNA methylation at specific CpG sites, to a single number. Roughly two hundred have been published since 2013, and they were not fitted to the same target. Some were regressed on calendar age, some on a survival-weighted composite and then rescaled into years, some on the rate of change in organ-system biomarkers tracked longitudinally, some on cumulative stem-cell divisions. Those are four different quantities. Reported together as “biological age” they look comparable, and the arithmetic that mixes them has no defined meaning.
This package treats that as the problem to solve rather than a caveat to mention. Every catalogue entry declares the target its clock was trained on, the unit the output carries, and which downstream operations are consequently defined. Asking for age acceleration on a pace-of-aging clock returns an error naming the units, not a number. Scoring a placenta clock on blood is refused. Scoring saliva on a whole-blood clock warns and cites the size of the error measured in people sampled both ways. The refusals are the design, and each one names the measurement it rests on.
The second half of the package is about what a single number is worth. Technical replicates of the same DNA differ by up to nine years on prominent clocks, and only 18% of probes on the 450K array reach an intraclass correlation of 0.5 in whole blood. A score reported without that context invites a reader to believe a difference that the assay alone could have produced. FALCONAge propagates published per-probe reliability through each clock’s own weights to give a standard error per sample, and calibrates distribution-free prediction intervals against known ages.
It is one numerical core in Python, called from R through reticulate, so a result obtained in either language is the same bits rather than two implementations that agree approximately. The catalogue holds 68 human clocks, and every one of them ships its coefficients and scores offline.
These are instruments for population research, not a clinical judgement about one person. FALCONAge computes what the papers specify and records how it did so; whether a given clock is fit for a given decision is not something a scoring tool can certify, and the limits below say what else it cannot do.

title: About and design
text:
Scope and limitations
What the tool is for, what it declines to do, and what it cannot do yet. Three different questions with three different answers, in the order a model card puts them.

Intended use
The reason, rather than the disclaimer. Reliability varies sharply between clocks, and technical reproducibility and biological stability are separate properties that do not track together: a clock can be highly repeatable on split samples and still move with a meal or a night’s sleep. So a score that survives replication is not thereby measuring a stable trait, and the two failures need different evidence to rule out. The science of aging clocks sets out, clock by clock, which is established and which is contested.


Out-of-scope use
Each gate is a place where the wrong answer is available and cheap. A clock scored on the wrong specimen, on too little of its own model, on a scale that does not admit the operation asked for, on clinical values whose units were never stated, or from a weights file that cannot be redistributed, all return a number that looks exactly like a right one. The output of the last gate is a score and a manifest recording which gates it passed and on what evidence.
Each of these is a silent wrong answer somewhere else, so each is a hard failure here:

Fill a missing probe with zero. In beta space zero means completely unmethylated, which is a real and extreme measurement. An absent feature takes the clock’s reference value: the authors’ own for Horvath 2013, DunedinPoAm38, CorticalClock and AltumAge, a healthy adult blood mean for 22 other blood clocks. Where there is none, it takes the mean of the clock’s present features, and the run names that fallback with the share of the weight it touched. Every substitution is counted in the manifest.
Guess clinical units. PhenoAge has SI and conventional variants that disagree by years. units= has no default.
Score below the coverage floor. A clock whose features are largely absent is skipped and named, rather than scored on mostly-imputed input.
Treat probes as interchangeable. Coverage is measured twice: by count, and by the share of the model’s total |coefficient| the present features carry. A clock can clear a 92% feature floor having lost the probes that do a third of the work, and only the second number sees it. probe_loss() reports both before you score anything.
Claim coverage means validity. High coverage says the probes are present. It says nothing about whether coefficients fitted in one tissue, species or population transfer to yours; that judgement stays with you, and Choosing a clock lays out the grounds for it.
Let a paper-versus-implementation disagreement pass silently. Eleven clocks in the catalogue are scored from coefficients that differ from what their paper describes: a feature count, a changed statistic, a constant. Each carries the note, and it is raised as a warning at score time, not left on a documentation page.



Known limitations
Said here rather than left to be inferred. Uncertainty and Preparing data and coverage cover each in full, with the algorithms and the reason each is or is not blocked.

It does not repair cross-platform probe loss. It measures it twice over: by count, by coefficient mass, and now in years per clock per platform. It cannot undo it. The liftover mapping tables encode concordance measured on paired samples and are not derivable from the array manifests.
It does not preprocess raw data. IDAT decoding, normalisation, detection filtering and sample QC belong to an array pipeline such as methylarray; FALCONAge reads the resulting beta matrix. Its own preparation is limited to identifier harmonisation, EPIC v2 replicate collapse and clipping.
It has no proteomic or transcriptomic clocks. No published model in either family may be redistributed, and proteomic and transcriptomic tables are not read.
It has no foundation-model backend. The NeuralClock architecture ships, safetensors only. CpGPT and MethylGPT are interesting here for zero-shot imputation and array conversion rather than as another age predictor.

Removed from this list, because it now exists: single-cell scoring.

title: The Claude skill
text:
The repository ships a Claude skill at .claude/skills/falconage/. It is four markdown files: the workflow (SKILL.md), the Docker command set, the clock catalogue routed by the question each clock answers, and every refusal with the measurement behind it.
It is active already for anyone working inside a clone. To have it available in any directory, copy it into your personal skills folder with cp -r .claude/skills/falconage ~/.claude/skills/, or on Windows PowerShell Copy-Item -Recurse .claude\skills\falconage $HOME\.claude\skills\.
Then ask in plain language. “Score this beta matrix and tell me which clocks you refused and why” is enough; the skill supplies the rest.






NoteWhy the skill is checked by CI, and checked harder than the prose



docs/check_api_docs.py resolves every fa.* name and every falconage <verb> in the skill against the running package on each push, exactly as it does for these pages.
The reason it matters more here is that these pages are read by a person, who notices when a function does not exist and goes looking. A skill is read by a model that then runs what it says. The first draft named five readers at top level that actually live under fa.preprocess, and invented a falconage probe verb outright, copied from a specification section of the architecture page that described a verb never built. The check caught all six, and then caught two more invented verbs on that page.

title: Add a clock
text: A clock of your own is a YAML entry and a coefficient file. Added to a run, it gets everything a catalogue clock gets: the coverage check, the specimen check, a technical standard error, a row in the report, and a manifest entry recording that it is yours and the SHA-256 of its file.

title: Add a clock
text:
1. Write the entry
my_clocks/mycohortclock.yaml:
id: mycohortclock
name: Cohort clock fitted on our blood samples
data_type: dna_methylation
tissue: [whole blood]
platform: [EPICv1]
training_target: [chronological age]
scale_type: age_years
unit: [years]
coefficients: mycohortclock.csv
reference: mycohortclock_reference.csv    # optional
my_clocks/mycohortclock.csv:
feature_id,coefficient
(Intercept),31.47
cg16867657,22.1
cg06639320,-14.8
Build a clock and Stack clocks write both files for you.







Field
Why it is required




scale_type
Decides which arithmetic is legal: age_years permits acceleration, a pace or a relative score does not


tissue
Drives the check that your samples are the specimen the clock was fitted on


training_target, unit
What the score estimates, and in what


coefficients
One weight per feature, with an optional (Intercept) row



Optional: platform, reference (a feature_id,value file of fill values for CpGs a dataset lacks), preprocess and postprocess steps by the names in the registry, citation, notes.

title: Add a clock
text:
2. Score it
From the command line, point run at the folder:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu \
  run betas.csv --samples samples.csv --clocks-dir my_clocks
From Python or R, add it for the session:

PythonR


fa.add_clock("my_clocks/mycohortclock.yaml")
res = fa.score(d, clocks=["mycohortclock", "horvath2013"])


add_clock("my_clocks/mycohortclock.yaml")
res <- score(d, clocks = c("mycohortclock", "horvath2013"))

title: Add a clock
section: What is checked, and what a clock of your own does not get
text:
What is checked, and what a clock of your own does not get
The coefficient file must have two columns, unique feature ids and finite values; processing steps must name operations FALCONAge implements; and the id may not replace a clock that ships with the package. A clock of your own has no published calibration, so it gets no prediction interval until you supply one, and no published reliability, so interpretation() says so.

title: FALCONAge
text:
FALCONAge applies 68 published human aging clocks to DNA methylation, clinical chemistry and NMR metabolomics data. Every clock ships its coefficients and runs offline. Each score is reported with its unit, the source of its coefficients and its technical standard error.
The input is data that is already preprocessed and quality controlled: a beta matrix from an array pipeline such as methylarray, a GEO series matrix, a clinical chemistry table or a Nightingale NMR table.

title: FALCONAge
text:
Run it in three commands
You need Docker and nothing else. Install covers Docker itself and other ways to install.
1. Get the image (once, about 430 MB to download):
docker pull bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu
2. See it work on a small synthetic dataset, in about a minute:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu demo
3. Run your own data. Put your beta matrix and, if you have one, a sample sheet with each sample’s age, sex and tissue in the current folder:
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/work" bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu run betas.csv --samples samples.csv
Open betas_falconage/report.html. Your first run explains every file the run writes and how to read the report.

title: FALCONAge
text:
Output

One score per sample per clock, for every catalogued clock the input supports
A technical standard error on every score, propagated from published per-probe reliability through each clock’s weights, and a distribution-free prediction interval
A coverage map of every clock’s CpGs across the genome, a coverage table per clock, and the expected shift in years caused by missing probes
A run manifest recording the package and registry versions, the SHA-256 of every coefficient file, the reliability table behind the intervals, the floating-point precision, the imputation policy and every warning raised

Execution. One numerical core in Python, called from R through reticulate, so a result is the same in either language.
Refusals. A saliva sample scored on a whole-blood clock (measured at 3.83–16.46 years of error in the same people). Cell-free DNA on any array clock. Age acceleration on a pace-of-aging clock. A cohort-centred clock given one sample. Each refusal names the measurement behind it.

title: Design history
text:
The requirement was one tool, Python and R, multiomic input, and correct, meaning it reproduces published clock values on published test vectors.
This section was the sketch that turned that into a design. It is now documented properly elsewhere, and the sketch has been cut rather than kept in parallel: it used the abandoned working name agingscore and an API that no longer exists, so anyone who copied from it got nothing that runs.
Architecture is the design record for the built system, and it is checked against the running package rather than remembered. Where to look:



What the blueprint specified
Where it is documented now

Implemented layout, the file tree

Core engine, the shipped FalconData, AnnData-backed


Clock registry schema
Clock registry, the schema as validated, field by field


API surface, Python and R
Getting started, and the Python and R references


Correctness strategy
New modules below, which is the part that did not reduce to an implementation detail


Packaging, distribution, CI
Docker, Existing software landscape


Build order and milestones
Prior implementations, with the exit criterion each milestone was held to



Two decisions from the blueprint are worth restating because they are about the field rather than about this package. Weights belong outside the git repository, in safetensors rather than pickles, because unpickling a file executes arbitrary code, and pickles are what several packages still accept. And a license field has to gate use and print at score time: a tool that redistributes weights must surface their licence rather than bury it.


This is the part that decides whether a clock implementation is trusted, and it is the reason the next subsection exists at all.

Gold-standard vectors. For every clock, an input matrix and the expected output from the original implementation, asserted to 1e-6 in FP64.
Cross-implementation agreement. Where two packages implement the same clock, compare, and record disagreements in the registry rather than picking a side silently. New registry artefacts is that record.
Registry validation against a controlled vocabulary for tissue, platform, predicts, training target, unit, data type, species, model type and population. With 161 entries there is no other way to keep them coherent.
Property tests. Proportions sum to 1; probabilities in [0,1]; monotone response to a synthetic age gradient; permuting feature order must not change results; adding a duplicated sample must not change either sample’s score.
Numerical dtype tests. FP32-versus-FP64 divergence held under a documented per-clock tolerance. The PC clocks are the ones to watch.

title: Design history
text:
Open questions
Clocks whose coefficients cannot be shipped. Research-use-only and untraceable coefficient sets are not in the registry. The answer for them is add_clock: a user who holds the coefficients and the right to use them adds the clock to their own registry, where it is scored, covered by the coverage map and recorded in the manifest like any shipped clock.
CRAN name. available::available("FALCONAge") has not been run. PyPI is clear for both falconage and FALCONAge. If CRAN objects, the Python name stays and only the R name moves.
How much benchmark data to vendor. ComputAgeBench is 10,404 samples across 65 studies, several gigabytes. Fetching on demand from Hugging Face keeps the package small but makes the benchmark untestable offline and in CI. Likely answer: vendor a small deterministic subset (3 studies, around 200 samples) for CI and tests, fetch the full set on demand.
IDAT parsing dependency. methylprep is the only maintained pure-Python IDAT reader, and it is a heavy dependency with an opinionated pipeline of its own. The alternatives are vendoring the IDAT binary parser (roughly 300 lines, well-specified format) or requiring R and minfi through rpy2. Leaning toward vendoring the parser and implementing noob and BMIQ natively, with methylprep as an optional accelerated path.
Which normalisation is the default. noob + BMIQ and SeSAMe both perform well and are not interchangeable. Defaulting to either makes results from the two paths incomparable while looking identical. Current plan is to require the choice explicitly on the first call and record it everywhere, with noob_bmiq as the documented default only because it is what most published clock coefficients were derived under.
Resolved (1.0.0): preprocessing moved upstream. The IDAT reader, noob, BMIQ, probe masks, frozen-reference batch correction and the proteomic and transcriptomic readers were built and then removed. Array preprocessing and QC are done by a dedicated pipeline (methylarray, minfi or SeSAMe), and FALCONAge reads its beta matrix. The two open questions above no longer apply.

title: Core engine and clock registry
text:
falconage/core/backend.py
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ComputeSpec:
    dtype: str = "float64"        # "float64" | "float32"

def resolve(dtype: str | None = None, *, requires_fp64: bool = False) -> ComputeSpec
Everything runs in numpy on the CPU. resolve() fixes the floating-point precision once per clock and the manifest records it per clock. An unknown precision is refused rather than silently replaced.
FP64 is the default because the reference values the tests assert against are generated at it. FP32 is opt-in. Clocks whose registry entry sets requires_fp64: true are promoted back to FP64 for their own forward pass and a warning is emitted.
def check_dtype_safety(clock: ClockMeta, spec: ComputeSpec) -> ComputeSpec:
    """Promote to FP64 for clocks that need it. Returns a possibly-modified spec."""



falconage/core/container.py
FalconData wraps anndata.AnnData rather than replacing it, so the on-disk artefact is a plain .h5ad that both languages and every scverse tool can read.
class FalconData:
    adata: AnnData                    # X = primary modality, obs = samples, var = features
    modality: str                     # "methylation" | "clinical" | "expression" | "proteomics"
    platform: str | None              # "illumina_450k" | "illumina_epic_v2" | ...
    species: str                      # "homo_sapiens" | ...
    units: dict[str, str]             # feature → unit, for clinical chemistry
Conventions, matching pyaging’s AnnData slot contract and extending it:







Slot
Content




X
samples × features, the primary modality


obs
age, sex, tissue, condition, subject_id, timepoint, time, status, plus predictions after scoring


var
feature_id, id_type, platform, chromosome, position


obsm["X_<clock>"]
transient per-clock feature slice, deleted after scoring unless keep=True


layers["<modality>"]
a second modality on the same features


uns["falconage"]
the run manifest


uns["<clock>_percent_na"], uns["<clock>_missing_features"], uns["<clock>_metadata"]
per-clock diagnostics



Multi-modality with different feature spaces (850K methylation probes alongside 3,000 proteins) uses MuData, with FalconData.from_mudata() / .to_mudata(). A single FalconData always has one primary feature space.
Constructors:
FalconData.from_dataframe(df, modality, platform=None, metadata_cols=(), units=None)
FalconData.from_anndata(adata, modality, ...)
FalconData.read_h5ad(path)
FalconData.write_h5ad(path)
from_dataframe takes samples in rows and features in columns, splits metadata_cols into obs, and preserves df.index as sample identifiers. This is the same signature as pyaging’s df_to_adata minus the imputation, which moves to the preprocess module where it belongs.



falconage/core/manifest.py
Everything needed to reproduce a run, written into uns["falconage"] and into a sidecar run_manifest.json next to the results.
@dataclass
class RunManifest:
    falconage_version:  str
    registry_version:   str

@dataclass(frozen=True)

    dtype: str = "float64"        # "float64" | "float32"

def resolve(dtype: str | None = None, *, requires_fp64: bool = False) -> ComputeSpec
Everything runs in numpy on the CPU. resolve() fixes the floating-point precision once per clock and the manifest records it per clock. An unknown precision is refused rather than silently replaced.

title: Core engine and clock registry
text:
Clock registry

Why the registry is a separate artefact
The registry is versioned independently of the package, packaged into both language distributions, and validated in its own CI job. That separation exists because adding a clock and releasing software are different events with different risk profiles: a user pinning registry_version: "1.0.0" gets the same coefficients in a year regardless of package upgrades, and a registry fix does not require a PyPI release.


Schema

v1.0 stores this differently. All 68 entries live in one file, python/src/falconage/registry/data/clocks.yaml, loaded into frozen dataclasses by registry/registry.py. There is no registry/ directory at the repository root, no file per clock, and no pydantic.
The per-clock tree below is the right shape for a registry that outside contributors edit concurrently, one file per pull request, no merge conflicts. At 68 entries maintained by one author it bought nothing and cost a directory walk on every import, plus 68 files to keep a schema version in step across. The single file is 68 entries the loader validates in one pass, and it travels inside the wheel so a clock catalogue is never a download. Pydantic went the same way: the fields are flat, the loader coerces and defaults them in about forty lines, and a runtime dependency that exists to check a file the package itself ships is a dependency earning nothing.
The entry below is copied from the shipped file; it is what the loader reads.

# one entry in falconage/registry/data/clocks.yaml
horvath2013:
  name: "horvath2013"
  year: 2013
  species: "Homo sapiens"
  data_type: "dna_methylation"
  generation: "first"
  tissue: ["multi-tissue"]
  platform: ["27K", "450K"]
  predicts: ["chronological age"]
  training_target: ["chronological age"]
  unit: ["years"]
  scale_type: "age_years"          # governs which downstream operations are legal
  model_type: "elastic net regression"
  population: "all ages"
  n_features: 353
  requires_fp64: false
  availability: "bundled"
  citation: "Horvath, S. DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types. Genome Biology 14, R115 (2013)."
  doi: "https://doi.org/10.1186/gb-2013-14-10-r115"
  coefficient_source:
    file: "coefficients/horvath2013.csv"
    sha256: "a54cdb931c85763ed8e28be68fa926b4e602be168df505683ea5c6b2ba3a5319"
    provenance: "Horvath 2013, Additional File 3 (publisher supplementary)"
    primary_source_traced: true
    redistributable: true
  reference_values:
    file: "references/horvath2013.csv"
    label: "Horvath 2013 gold standard (Additional file 22)"
  preprocess: []
  postprocess:                     # order is load-bearing
    - {op: "add", value: 0.695507258}
    - {op: "anti_log_linear", adult_age: 20}


The discrepancy field is load-bearing
Where the paper and the coefficients disagree documents the clocks where the published paper and the coefficient set in circulation disagree. Every implementation in the field silently inherits one side of each disagreement. FALCONAge records both and warns at score time:
# bohlin, as shipped
known_discrepancies:
  - "The paper reports 96 CpGs; the coefficient set in circulation carries 251. Scores here
    will match other packages and not the figures printed in the paper."
Seventeen shipped clocks carry the field: bohlin, phenoage, weidner, zhangmortality, the three Ying clocks (yingcausage, yingdamage, yingadaptage) and the ten McCartney trait scores. Where the paper and the coefficients disagree gives each one.
Warning behaviour is a config knob: discrepancy_warnings: once | always | never, defaulting to once per clock per session.


Controlled vocabulary
registry/vocabulary.yaml fixes the allowed values for data_type, species, tissue, platform, population, generation, predicts, training_target, unit, scale_type and architecture.kind. A controlled vocabulary is what keeps tissue and platform filters working: free-text tissue strings drift into dozens of spellings of the same thing. registry/validate.py fails CI on any value outside the vocabulary, any missing required field, any weight URI without a checksum, and any clock without a gold-standard vector.


Registry API
falconage/registry/registry.py
class ClockRegistry:
    @classmethod
    def load(cls, version: str | None = None) -> ClockRegistry

    def get(self, clock_id: str) -> ClockMeta
    def list(self) -> list[str]
    def search(self, query: str) -> list[ClockMeta]          # free text over name, citation, notes
    def filter(self, **criteria) -> list[ClockMeta]          # data_type=, species=, generation=, ...
    def by_doi(self, doi: str) -> list[ClockMeta]
    def compatible_with(self, data: FalconData,
                        min_coverage: float = 0.8) -> list[ClockMeta]
    def cite(self, clock_id: str, style: str = "plain") -> str
compatible_with is the function that makes the registry usable: hand it a loaded dataset and it returns the clocks whose species, platform and feature coverage actually match, sorted by coverage. This replaces the current field practice of running everything and reading the missingness column afterwards.


Coefficient provenance and the three availability tiers
A clock is two things: an architecture, which is a procedure described in a paper, and a coefficient set, which is data produced by fitting that procedure to a cohort. FALCONAge writes every architecture from scratch. It cannot write a coefficient set from scratch, because there is no procedure that regenerates Horvath’s 353 weights without Horvath’s training data.
So the question for each clock is only ever where do its numbers come from and may we ship them. Copying a copy is how a transcription error becomes a field-wide convention, so every shipped set is traced back to its primary source, a publisher supplement or the authors’ own repository, and coefficient_source.provenance names it.
The registry schema keeps three values of availability: bundled (coefficients ship and score offline), untraced (no primary source established) and licensed (the coefficients are not FALCONAge’s to give). Every shipped clock is bundled. Clocks whose coefficients are research-use-only or untraceable were removed rather than catalogued without numbers, so nothing in the registry is a placeholder. The other two values remain so that a user’s own entry can say what it is. pedbe is the one bundled clock whose primary source is not fully traced, and falconage clocks list --untraced prints it.
coefficient_source:
  file: "coefficients/hannum.csv"
  sha256: "58d84337d3100888358763cd79c29a776e5cfdc675af99c14a339595aceaf375"
  provenance: "Hannum et al. 2013, Molecular Cell, Table S3 (mmc2.xlsx, sheet Model_PrimaryData)"
  primary_source_traced: true
  redistributable: true


Coefficient extraction
registry/extractors/. One small script per clock, or per family where the format is shared. Each reads the primary source in whatever shape it was published, xlsx, csv, a zip of csvs, an RData object, a supplementary PDF table, and emits a normalised two-column file plus a provenance record.
registry/extractors/
├── _base.py                 # fetch, checksum, normalise, write, record
├── horvath2013.py           # Springer MOESM3 csv
├── hannum.py                # Elsevier mmc2.xlsx, sheet 2, cols B:C
├── ying.py                  # Nature Aging MOESM6 zip, three clocks in one archive
└── ...
class Extractor(ABC):
    clock_id: str
    source_url: str
    expected_sha256: str
    expected_n_features: int

    @abstractmethod
    def parse(self, raw: bytes) -> pd.DataFrame:      # feature_id, coefficient
        ...

    def run(self) -> ExtractionResult:
        # fetch -> verify checksum -> parse -> assert n_features -> assert no
        # duplicate feature ids -> compare against any prior extraction -> write
Two assertions do most of the work. expected_n_features catches a supplement whose layout changed or a sheet index that was off by one. The comparison against the prior extraction turns an upstream file being silently revised into a failed CI run rather than a changed result.
Diffing against the field. For every clock where biolearn, computage or methylCIPHER also carries coefficients, the test suite compares the sets: features present in one and not the other, and coefficients differing beyond 1e-9. Disagreements are published rather than resolved silently.


Weight loading
falconage/registry/registry.py, methods of ClockRegistry:
def coefficients(self, clock_id: str) -> tuple[list[str], np.ndarray]
def intercept(self, clock_id: str) -> float
def weight_record(self, clock_id: str) -> dict[str, Any]          # what the manifest records
def register_local_weights(self, clock_id: str, path, sha256: str | None = None) -> str
def add_clock(self, path, *, replace: bool = False) -> str
Rules:

safetensors only. Loading a pickled weights file executes arbitrary code from a downloaded file. Architecture lives in the registry YAML and in models/; tensors live in safetensors; nothing pickled is ever loaded.
Checksum verified against the registry before use; a mismatch raises rather than warns.
Bundled. Every coefficient set ships inside the package, about 13 MB in all, so scoring never needs a network.
Your own weights: register_local_weights and add_clock take a local file, checksum it and record weight_record.source = "user_clock" in the manifest.

title: 8. R package
text:
FALCONAge is not a reimplementation. Every number it returns is computed by the Python core through reticulate, so the R and Python answers are the same bytes because they are the same computation. What the R package adds is an interface an R user would have written: S3 classes with print, summary, plot and as.data.frame; data.frame in and data.frame out; roxygen2 documentation; a pkgdown site; and errors that arrive as R conditions rather than Python tracebacks.
The R package does not reimplement anything, and it does not ask the user to set RETICULATE_PYTHON by hand: FALCONAge manages the environment itself.

title: 8. R package
text:
Environment management
R/install.R
falconage_install(method = c("auto", "uv", "virtualenv", "conda"),
                  envname = "r-falconage",
                  version = NULL,        # NULL = the version matching this R package
                  force = FALSE)

falconage_config()      # what Python, what version, what registry
falconage_available()   # logical, does a working core exist
falconage_update()
method = "auto" prefers uv when it is on the PATH, because it resolves in seconds rather than minutes, and falls back to virtualenv.
version = NULL pins the Python core to the exact version that matches the R package, read from DESCRIPTION’s Config/falconage/python-version field. This is the mechanism that stops an R package from silently driving a Python core it was never tested against.
falconage_config() prints the same block the CLI prints, so a bug report from an R user and one from a Python user carry comparable information:
FALCONAge 1.0.0 (R)
  python core   1.0.0  /home/x/.virtualenvs/r-falconage/bin/python
  dtype         float64
  registry      1.1.0  (68 human clocks)
  cache         /home/x/.cache/falconage  (2.1 GB)

title: 8. R package
text:
The bridge
R/zzz.R and R/bridge.R
.falconage <- new.env(parent = emptyenv())

.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  .falconage$py <- reticulate::import("falconage", delay_load = list(
    environment = "r-falconage",
    on_load  = function() check_version_compatibility(),
    on_error = function(e) NULL          # defer the error to first use
  ))
  set_default_options()
}
delay_load matters: without it, library(FALCONAge) fails on a machine with no Python environment yet, which breaks R CMD check on CRAN’s build farm. With it, the package loads, falconage_available() returns FALSE, and every exported function that needs the core calls require_core(), which raises a condition telling the user to run falconage_install().
Type marshalling. Explicit, never implicit.








R
Python

both: the object is passed as a file path, never marshalled cell by cell

The falcon_data rule is the important one. Passing an 850,000-column matrix through reticulate cell by cell is slow and copies twice. Instead the R object holds a path to an .h5ad file plus a cached summary (dimensions, platform, sample table), and both languages read the same file. This is also what makes a mixed-language workflow possible: preprocess in R, score in Python, plot back in R, one artefact throughout.
Error translation. bridge.R wraps every call:
py_call <- function(fn, ...) {
  tryCatch(fn(...), error = function(e) {
    info <- parse_python_error(e)      # class, message, .remedy
    rlang::abort(
      message = info$message,
      class   = paste0("falconage_", info$class),
      remedy  = info$remedy,
      parent  = e
    )
  })
}
A MissingUnitsError from Python becomes an R condition of class falconage_missing_units_error, so R users can tryCatch on it, and the message is the one-sentence remedy rather than a 40-line traceback. The Python traceback stays available as parent.

Description: Scores DNA methylation, clinical chemistry and NMR data against a
    catalogue of 68 published human aging clocks, and provides the downstream
    statistics the field expects: age acceleration in its three conventions,
    survival and association models, technical reliability, and the AA1/AA2
    benchmark. Numerical work is delegated to the 'falconage' Python package
    through 'reticulate', so results from R and from Python are the same bits
    rather than two implementations that agree approximately. Every
    clock carries its coefficients inside the package and runs offline.

    https://bhagesh-h.github.io/FALCONAge/,
    https://bhagesh-h.github.io/FALCONAge/r

    stats,

Encoding: UTF-8

Four departures from the specification, each deliberate:








Specified
Shipped
Why




ggplot2, cli, rlang, jsonlite in Imports
ggplot2 in Suggests; the other three absent
Plotting returns a data frame and draws with base graphics, so grDevices is the hard dependency and ggplot2 is optional. Four fewer required packages is four fewer ways for a CRAN check to fail on a machine we do not control.


Methods implemented include ... <doi:...> in the description
Absent
CRAN wants DOIs for methods the package implements in R. Every method here is implemented in the Python core; the per-clock references live in the registry and come back from cite(), which is a truer place for them than a fixed list of five.


SystemRequirements: Python (>= 3.10) ...
Absent
On reticulate ≥ 1.41 the environment is provisioned automatically on first use, so Python is not a system requirement the user must satisfy. Still to be added before a CRAN submission, since the field is also documentation.


Config/falconage/python-version
Absent
The R package pins the Python core by git tag inside falconage_install(), so the field would be a second copy of a number that already exists in one place.



Every example and every test that needs the core is wrapped in skip_if_not(falconage_available()), so R CMD check passes on a machine with no Python.

title: 8. R package
text:
Roxygen conventions
Following the cyRAVEN register, see R/thresholds.R in that package for the model. Every exported function gets:

an opening paragraph saying what it does, then why it does it that way when the choice is not obvious
@param on every argument, naming the unit or the allowed values
@return on every export, describing the object rather than naming its class
@examples, runnable, wrapped in \donttest{} when they need the core or the network
@seealso linking the Python equivalent by name
@references with the DOI for anything implementing a published method

Worked example:
#' Score biological age with one or more aging clocks
#'
#' WHAT: applies published aging-clock definitions to a prepared dataset and
#' returns one value per sample per clock, with the provenance needed to
#' interpret it.
#'
#' WHY THE DEFAULT IS `"compatible"` RATHER THAN `"all"`: the registry holds
#' clocks for several species, platforms and molecular layers, and most of them
#' do not apply to any given dataset. Running everything produces a table whose
#' majority of rows were computed almost entirely from imputed reference values,
#' which looks like a result and is not one. `"compatible"` selects the clocks
#' whose species, platform and feature coverage actually match the data, and
#' reports what it excluded.
#'
#' @param data A `falcon_data` object from [preprocess_methylation()] or
#'   [preprocess_clinical()].
#' @param clocks Clock identifiers, or `"compatible"` (default) to select
#'   automatically, or `"all"`. See [list_clocks()].
#' @param dtype `"float64"` (default) or `"float32"`. Clocks whose registry
#'   entry requires double precision are promoted regardless, with a warning.
#' @param max_missing Largest fraction of a clock's features that may be absent
#'   before scoring that clock is an error rather than a warning. Default 0.30.
#' @param sex_unknown What to do when a clock needs sex and it is not recorded:
#'   `"error"` (default), `"impute_from_methylation"`, or `"half"`.
#'
#' @return A `falcon_result`. [as.data.frame()] gives one row per sample per
#'   clock with the value, its unit, its scale type, the fraction of features
#'   that had to be imputed, and any flags raised. The underlying dataset,
#'   including the run manifest, is reachable through the object.
#'
#' @examples
#' \donttest{
#' if (falconage_available()) {
#'   data <- preprocess_methylation(
#'     system.file("extdata", "example_betas.csv", package = "FALCONAge"),
#'     platform = "illumina_450k"
#'   )
#'   res <- score(data, clocks = c("horvath2013", "phenoage"))
#'   head(as.data.frame(res))
#' }
#' }
#'
#' @seealso [acceleration()] for age acceleration, [list_clocks()] to browse the
#'   registry, and the Python equivalent `falconage.score()`.
#' @references
#' Horvath S (2013). DNA methylation age of human tissues and cell types.
#' Genome Biology 14:R115. \doi{10.1186/gb-2013-14-10-r115}
#' @export
score <- function(data, clocks = "compatible",
                  dtype = "float64", max_missing = 0.30,
                  sex_unknown = "error", ...) { }

title: 8. R package
text:
Command-line front end
inst/scripts/falconage.R, invoked the cyRAVEN way:
Rscript "$(Rscript -e 'cat(system.file("scripts","falconage.R",package="FALCONAge"))')" \
  score --input prepared.h5ad --clocks horvath2013,hannum --outdir results/
Options are built in R/cli-options.R with optparse, and the flag names match the Python CLI exactly, so a script written against one runs against the other with only the interpreter changed.

title: Docker, testing, documentation and CI
text:
One Dockerfile, docker/Dockerfile.cpu, with two build targets. The files themselves carry the reasoning in their comments; this section summarises them rather than copying them, so there is one copy to keep current.











Tag
Target
Contains
Size




bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-cpu, latest
full (default)
Python core with every reader, R and the FALCONAge package, the CLI
1.55 GB


bhagesh/falconage:1.0.0-py
py
Python core with plotting and spreadsheets, the CLI; no R, no parquet or .h5ad
0.84 GB



Sizes are uncompressed, as docker images reports them.




A pinned base and a lock file. python:3.12-slim-bookworm, and Python packages from python/uv.lock installed with --require-hashes, so a rebuild resolves the same versions. The dependency layer is copied before the source, so editing the source does not re-download anything.
R in two stages. Some R packages compile on install, which needs a C compiler and headers (about 0.5 GB). They are installed in an r-build stage, from a dated Posit binary snapshot, and only the finished library in /usr/local/lib/R/site-library is copied into the image. docker/install_deps.R reads r/DESCRIPTION, so the image can never install a different set than the package declares.
The CRAN signing key by fingerprint, as published on CRAN’s Debian page, never by short ID.
No build-time checks and no test tools in the published image. The test suite is run on demand (see Testing against the public corpus).
A non-root user, falcon (uid 1000), so files written to a mounted folder stay deletable.




Three jobs: a mounted checkout named by FALCONAGE_SOURCE takes precedence over the installed copy, so an edit-run cycle needs no rebuild; a bare docker run prints help; and python, R, Rscript, sh and bash as the first argument run that program instead of a falconage verb.



Three services: falconage (the published image, with a build: to reproduce it), falconage-dev (the same image with the checkout mounted and FALCONAGE_SOURCE set) and testdata (the small image that fetches the public test corpus). A named volume keeps downloaded manifests and data between runs.
